docs.section: Agentic architecture: from one LLM call to multi-agent systems
docs.text: AI · Topic 3 · Exam domain D1 Agentic architecture: from one LLM call to multi-agent systems An agent is a model that uses tools in a loop to reach a goal, choosing its own next step. This page builds the idea up from a single API call: the agent loop, when not to build an agent, the five workflow patterns, multi-agent orchestration, context engineering, memory, and how to make agents reliable. Each idea comes with an animated diagram or tested code. D1 27% of the exam 3 animated diagrams 4 runnable code files ≈ 75 min read

docs.keywords: definition autonomy spectrum workflow agent llm tools loop environment
docs.text: A plain LLM call is a function: text in, text out. It can't look anything up, change anything, or check its own work. An agent wraps the model in a loop and gives it tools. It reads the situation, chooses an action, sees what happened, and repeats until the goal is met. Working definitionAgent = model + tools + a loop + an environment, where the model decides the next step. If your code decides every step, you've built a workflow instead. That's often the better choice. 🧠 Model (brain) Reasons about the goal, picks the next action, and judges when it's done. Claude emits tool_use blocks; it never executes anything itself. 🛠️ Tools (hands) Functions the model may call: search, read a file, run tests, send an email. Their names, descriptions, and schemas are the model's whole picture of what it can do. 🔁 Loop & harness (body) Your code: calls the model, runs the tools it asks for, feeds results back, enforces limits and permissions. See Harness Engineering. 🗂️ Context & memory Everything the model can see on this turn (instructions, history, tool results), plus anything saved outside the window (files, memory stores). The autonomy spectrum Move right only when the task needs it. Each step to the right buys flexibility and costs predictability, latency, and tokens.

headings: How your code knows what to do next: stop_reason
The same agent with the SDK's tool runner
docs.keywords: loop stop_reason tool_use end_turn tool_result runner
docs.text: Every agent, from a 30-line script to Claude Code, runs the same loop. The model sees the context, either answers or asks for a tool, your code runs the tool, the result is appended, and the model looks again. The green dot is one iteration. Each lap costs a model call. When the model has nothing more to do it ends the turn (dashed arrow) instead of asking for a tool. How your code knows what to do next: stop_reason stop_reason Meaning Your loop should… tool_use The model wants one or more tools run Execute every tool_use block and send all results back in one user message end_turn The model is done Return the answer, or verify it first (tests, checks) max_tokens The output hit your max_tokens cap Raise the cap, or ask it to continue. Don't treat a truncated answer as done pause_turn A long-running server tool paused the turn Send the conversation back unchanged so it can resume refusal Safety classifiers declined the request Stop; read stop_details; don't retry blindly stop_sequence A custom stop string was produced Handle per your protocol The loop, written by hand A complete support agent with two tools. The numbered comments are the six rules every hand-written loop must follow. """The agent loop, written by hand: the model decides, your code executes.""" import json import anthropic client = anthropic.Anthropic() MODEL = "claude-opus-5-5" TOOLS = [ { "name": "get_order", "description": ( "Look up a customer order by ID. Returns status, items and ship date as JSON. " "Use it whenever the customer mentions an order number such as 'A-1042'." ), "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": {"order_id": {"type": "string", "description": "Order ID, e.g. A-1042"}}, "required": ["order_id"], "additionalProperties": False, }, "strict": True, }, { "name": "refund_order", "description": "Refund a delivered order. Only call after get_order confirms it was delivered.", "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "order_id": {"type": "string"}, "reason": {"type": "string", "enum": ["damaged", "late", "not_as_described"]}, }, "required": ["order_id", "reason"], "additionalProperties": False, }, "strict": True, }, ] ORDERS = {"A-1042": {"status": "delivered", "items": ["kettle"], "shipped": "2026-10-01"}} def run_tool(name: str, args: dict) -> str: if name == "get_order": order = ORDERS.get(args["order_id"]) if order is None: raise LookupError(f"No order {args['order_id']}. Ask the customer to re-check the ID.") return json.dumps(order) if name == "refund_order": return json.dumps({"refunded": True, "order_id": args["order_id"], "reason": args["reason"]}) raise ValueError(f"Unknown tool: {name}") def run_agent(task: str, max_turns: int = 10) -> str: messages = [{"role": "user", "content": task}] for _ in range(max_turns): # 1. hard stop: never loop forever response = client.messages.create( model=MODEL, max_tokens=16000, system="You are a support agent. Always verify an order before refunding it.", tools=TOOLS, messages=messages, ) messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content}) # 2. keep ALL blocks if response.stop_reason != "tool_use": # 3. end_turn, max_tokens, refusal ... return "".join(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text") results = [] for block in response.content: # 4. there may be several calls (parallel) if block.type != "tool_use": continue try: output, failed = run_tool(block.name, block.input), False except Exception as exc: # 5. errors go back to the model, not up the stack output, failed = f"Error: {exc}", True results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id, "content": output, "is_error": failed}) messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results}) # 6. all results in ONE message return "Stopped: turn limit reached." if __name__ == "__main__": print(run_agent("My kettle from order A-1042 arrived cracked. Can I get a refund?")) ⚠️ The classic loop bugs Appending only the text of the assistant reply. You must append the full response.content, because the tool_use blocks (and thinking blocks) have to be there for the tool_result ids to match. One message per tool result. When the model makes parallel calls, return all results in one user message. Splitting them teaches the model to stop making parallel calls. Raising on tool errors. A failed tool should return is_error: true with a helpful message. The model can usually recover; a crashed loop can't. No turn limit. Agents can loop. Always cap turns, tokens, or dollars. The same agent with the SDK's tool runner In most projects you don't hand-write the loop. The Python SDK's tool_runner (beta) builds each tool's schema from the function signature and docstring, then runs the call → execute → append cycle for you: """Same agent, but the SDK's tool runner owns the loop. You only write tools.""" import json import anthropic from anthropic import beta_tool client = anthropic.Anthropic() ORDERS = {"A-1042": {"status": "delivered", "items": ["kettle"]}} @beta_tool def get_order(order_id: str) -> str: """Look up a customer order by ID and return its status as JSON. Args: order_id: Order ID, e.g. A-1042. """ return json.dumps(ORDERS.get(order_id, {"error": f"no order {order_id}"})) @beta_tool def refund_order(order_id: str, reason: str) -> str: """Refund a delivered order. Only call after get_order confirms delivery. Args: order_id: Order ID, e.g. A-1042. reason: One of damaged, late, not_as_described. """ return json.dumps({"refunded": True, "order_id": order_id}) if __name__ == "__main__": runner = client.beta.messages.tool_runner( model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=16000, tools=[get_order, refund_order], messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Order A-1042 arrived damaged. Refund it please."}], ) for message in runner: # one iteration per model turn; stops when Claude is done for block in message.content: if block.type == "text": print(block.text) Write the loop by hand when you need control the runner doesn't give you. Otherwise prefer the runner. Its per-turn hooks still let you add approvals and logging.

docs.section: 3. Workflows vs agents: choose the simplest thing that works
docs.keywords: when to use agent workflow decision simplest
docs.text: The most common architecture mistake is building an agent when a workflow would do. A workflow runs LLM calls along paths your code defines. An agent lets the model choose the path. Workflows are cheaper, faster, and much easier to test. Agents are for problems whose steps you can't predict in advance. Ask If "no"… Complexity: Is the task multi-step and hard to fully specify in advance? Use a single call or a fixed workflow Value: Does the outcome justify extra cost and latency (agents use many more tokens)? Use a workflow with a cheaper model Viability: Is the model actually good at this kind of task? Narrow the task or keep a human in the loop Cost of error: Can mistakes be caught and undone (tests, review, rollback)? Add approval gates, or don't automate it 🎯 Exam lensWhen a scenario has known, fixed steps (extract → validate → format), the right answer is almost always a workflow or prompt chain, not an autonomous agent. Pick an agent when the path depends on what is discovered along the way (debugging, research, open-ended coding).

headings: Why it works, and what it costs
Subagents with the Claude Agent SDK
docs.keywords: subagents orchestrator lead agent delegation context isolation handoff parallel
docs.text: A multi-agent system is orchestrator–workers where the workers are themselves agents: each subagent runs its own loop with its own tools and its own context window. The lead agent plans, delegates, and combines condensed results. Big orange dots = task briefs going out. Bars = each subagent's private context filling up as it works. Small green dots = short summaries coming back. The lead's context stays clean. Why it works, and what it costs ✅ Benefits Context isolation: each subagent explores in a fresh window and returns a condensed result (often around 1–2k tokens), so the lead's context stays focused. Parallelism: independent research threads run at the same time. Specialisation: different prompts, tools, and models per role (e.g. a read-only reviewer). ⚠️ Costs Tokens: Anthropic reported its multi-agent research system used roughly 15× the tokens of a chat. Use it only where the value justifies that. Coordination: subagents can duplicate work or misread vague briefs. Poor fit for tightly coupled work where every agent needs the same evolving state (e.g. many agents editing the same files). Writing a good subagent brief ObjectiveOne concrete goal: "Find the three most-cited 2025 papers on X", not "research X". Output formatExactly what to return and how long. The lead must be able to merge it. Tools & sourcesWhich tools to use and which to avoid; where to look first. BoundariesWhat is out of scope, plus effort limits ("stop after ~10 tool calls"), so subagents don't overlap or sprawl. Subagents with the Claude Agent SDK The Agent SDK packages Claude Code's harness as a library. Subagents are declared with AgentDefinition and launched by the model through the built-in Agent tool. In Claude Code itself, the equivalent is a Markdown file in .claude/agents/. """A full agent with built-in tools and a subagent, using the Claude Agent SDK.""" import asyncio from claude_agent_sdk import AgentDefinition, ClaudeAgentOptions, ResultMessage, query options = ClaudeAgentOptions( model="claude-opus-5-5", system_prompt="You are a careful senior engineer. Read code before changing it.", allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "Edit", "Bash", "Agent"], permission_mode="acceptEdits", # edits auto-approved; other risky tools still ask max_turns=40, # hard stop for the loop max_budget_usd=2.00, # hard stop for spend agents={ "test-runner": AgentDefinition( description="Runs the test suite and reports failures. Use after every code change.", prompt="Run the tests. Report ONLY failing tests as file:line plus the error message.", tools=["Bash", "Read"], model="haiku", # cheaper model for a narrow job ), }, ) async def main() -> None: async for message in query(prompt="Fix the failing date-parsing test in src/", options=options): if isinstance(message, ResultMessage): print(message.result) print(f"turns={message.num_turns} cost=${message.total_cost_usd}") if __name__ == "__main__": asyncio.run(main()) Two communication shapesHub-and-spoke (shown above): subagents only talk to the lead, which keeps control and context clean. Handoff / peer-to-peer: one agent passes the whole conversation to another, which suits phase changes (triage → specialist). Default to hub-and-spoke; it's easier to debug.

docs.keywords: context window context rot compaction just in time retrieval notes attention budget
docs.text: The context window is the agent's working memory, and it's a finite attention budget. As it fills with stale tool output and old turns, quality drops ("context rot") and cost rises. Context engineering means deciding what goes into the window on every turn. Orange = conversation history. Without management it reaches the limit. With compaction, the oldest turns become a summary (green) and the agent keeps going. Five techniques Technique What it does Example Just-in-time retrieval Keep lightweight references (paths, URLs, IDs) and load content with tools only when needed Claude Code uses glob/grep to find files instead of pasting the whole repo Compaction Summarise old turns when nearing the limit API server-side compaction (compact_20260112); Claude Code's auto-compact Clearing stale tool results Drop old, already-used tool outputs from the window Context editing (clear_tool_uses_20250919) Structured note-taking The agent writes progress, decisions, and to-dos to a file and re-reads it later NOTES.md, a progress file, the memory tool Subagent isolation Push exploration into a subagent; only its summary comes back The multi-agent pattern above 💡 Rule of thumbFind the smallest set of high-signal tokens that lets the model do the next step well. More context isn't better context.

docs.section: 7. Memory: what survives the context window
docs.keywords: memory short term long term memory tool CLAUDE.md episodic semantic procedural
docs.text: Kind Lives in Lifetime Examples Working memory The context window One session (until compacted) Conversation, tool results, current plan Procedural (how to work) Instruction files loaded at start Persistent, versioned CLAUDE.md, skills, system prompts Episodic (what happened) Files or stores the agent writes Across sessions Progress logs, git history, session summaries Semantic (facts) External stores queried by tools Long-term The memory tool (memory_20250818, a /memories directory you host), a database, or a vector index for RAG ⚠️ TrapThe model itself is stateless. It remembers nothing between API calls. "Memory" always means the harness puts text back into the prompt, either up front (instruction files) or on demand (a tool reads it).

docs.keywords: ReAct plan and execute reflection thinking adaptive effort
docs.text: Pattern How it works Use it when ReAct (reason + act) Think → act (tool) → observe → think… This is the default agent loop Almost always; it's the baseline Plan-and-execute Write an explicit plan first (often a to-do list), then work through it, re-planning when reality differs Long tasks; when a human should approve the plan (Claude Code's plan mode) Reflection / self-critique After acting, the agent (or a separate grader) checks the result against criteria and revises Quality-sensitive outputs (the evaluator–optimizer pattern) Extended reasoning Adaptive thinking lets the model reason privately before and between tool calls; output_config.effort trades depth against cost Hard decisions inside the loop; turn effort up for coding and agentic work, down for simple routing

headings: Design checklist for a new agent
docs.keywords: failure modes guardrails human in the loop idempotent verification infinite loop prompt injection
docs.text: Failure mode Symptom Architectural fix Runaway loops Same tool called again and again; cost spikes Turn/token/dollar budgets; detect repeated identical calls Premature "done" Agent declares success without checking Verification step (tests, checks) before accepting end_turn Goal drift Long sessions wander from the task Written plan or to-do list re-read each step; progress notes Tool misuse Wrong tool, malformed arguments Better tool names/descriptions, strict: true schemas, fewer overlapping tools Irreversible mistakes Deleted data, sent emails, pushed to main Human approval gates for destructive actions; sandboxes; dry-run modes Prompt injection A web page or file tells the agent to do something else Treat tool output as data; least-privilege tools; approvals; never give one agent private data + untrusted input + a way to send data out Context overflow / rot Quality drops late in long sessions Compaction, clearing, notes, subagents (section 6) 🎯 Exam lensGuardrails that must always hold (never push to main, never delete outside the workspace) belong in deterministic code: hooks, permission rules, sandboxes. They don't belong only in the prompt. Prompts guide behaviour; code enforces it. Design checklist for a new agent Prove it needs to be an agentTry a single call or a workflow first (section 3). Define doneA checkable success condition (tests pass, schema valid, human approves). Design a small tool setFew, well-described, non-overlapping tools (see Tool Design & MCP). Set limitsMax turns, tokens or dollars, and wall-clock time. Gate the dangerous actionsPermissions, approvals, sandbox. Plan for contextRetrieval strategy, compaction, notes, subagents. Observe and evaluateTrace every step; run a fixed task set on every change (see Harness Engineering).

Score: 0 / 0 answered 1 · An invoice pipeline always does: extract fields → validate totals → format JSON. Which architecture fits best? B. The steps are fixed and known in advance, so code should own the flow. A gate between steps catches errors cheaply. An agent adds cost and unpredictability for no benefit. 2 · Claude returns three tool_use blocks in one response. How should the loop reply? C. Every tool_use needs a matching tool_result (failures included, with is_error), all in a single message. 3 · What is the main reason to give a research task to subagents rather than one long-running agent? A. Context isolation (plus parallelism) is the point. Total token use usually goes up, often by a lot. 4 · An agent must never run git push --force. Where should that rule be enforced? D. Prompts are guidance and can be ignored or injected against. Hooks and permission rules are guarantees. 5 · Late in a long session the agent's answers degrade, and the transcript is full of old file dumps. Best first fix? B. This is context rot. A bigger window delays the problem but doesn't remove the noise; max_tokens only limits output length. 6 · Which pattern fits "translate legal text until a reviewer finds no issues, max 3 rounds"? C. Generate, grade against criteria, revise, with a bounded loop. 7 · Your loop receives stop_reason: "max_tokens". What does it mean? A. Raise max_tokens or ask it to continue, and never treat it as a completed answer. Tool calls give tool_use; normal completion gives end_turn. 8 · An orchestrator–workers system differs from plain parallelization because… D. In sectioning, your code defines the sub-tasks. An orchestrator plans them based on the input.

docs.section: Claude Code — the complete architect's guide
docs.text: Claude Certification · Topic 6 · Exam domains D1, D2, D5 Claude Code — the complete architect's guide Claude Code is an agentic coding harness: a model running in a loop, with tools, permissions, memory and extension points around it. The exam tests whether you know which extension point solves a given problem and why. D1 Agentic architecture 27% D2 Claude Code config & workflows 20% D5 Context & reliability 15% ≈ 60–90 min read

Claude Code wraps a Claude model in a harness. The model decides what to do. The harness carries it out: it runs tools, enforces permissions, loads memory, fires hooks, and manages context. 🧠 Model Reasons, plans, and emits tool_use blocks. It never touches your machine directly. 🔁 Loop Calls the model, runs the requested tools, feeds results back, and repeats until stop_reason is end_turn. 🧰 Tools Read, Edit, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob, WebFetch, Agent… plus any MCP tools. 📜 Context System prompt, CLAUDE.md memory, skill descriptions, conversation, and tool results — all within one context window. 🛡 Guardrails Permission rules and modes, hooks, managed settings, sandboxing. 🧩 Extensions Skills, slash commands, subagents, hooks, MCP servers, plugins. Where it runs Terminal CLI (claude): the interactive REPL, or headless with claude -p. IDE extensions: VS Code (and forks), JetBrains. They share the CLI's config. Desktop app and web (claude.ai/code): cloud sessions in a sandbox. CI/CD: GitHub Actions (anthropics/claude-code-action), GitLab, or any pipeline through claude -p. Claude Agent SDK (Python / TypeScript): the same harness, used as a library to build your own agents. The same configuration files (CLAUDE.md, .claude/settings.json, .claude/skills, .claude/agents, .mcp.json) apply on every surface. 🎯 Exam lens Most D2 questions read as "a team wants X — what's the best mechanism?" Match the problem to the tool: always-on knowledge → CLAUDE.md, on-demand procedure → skill, isolated context / parallel work → subagent, must-happen-every-time → hook, external system → MCP, allow/deny actions → permissions.

docs.keywords: stop_reason end_turn tool_use max_tokens pause_turn refusal loop
docs.text: Every agent, Claude Code included, comes down to the same loop on the Messages API. The model replies with content blocks plus a stop_reason field that says why it stopped generating. Your code decides whether to loop by reading stop_reason, not by reading the text. The loop continues while stop_reason == "tool_use" and ends on end_turn. Every stop_reason value stop_reason Meaning What your loop should do end_turn The model finished its turn naturally. Stop. Return the final answer. tool_use The model wants one or more tools run. Run every tool_use block. Send all results back in one user message as tool_result blocks with matching tool_use_id. Call the model again. max_tokens The output hit your max_tokens cap. The response is truncated. Don't treat it as complete. Raise max_tokens or ask the model to continue. A cut-off tool_use block is invalid. stop_sequence The output matched one of your custom stop_sequences. Read response.stop_sequence and handle it in your application. pause_turn The API paused a long-running turn (usually with server tools such as web search). Send the response back unchanged as the assistant turn so the model can continue. refusal The model declined for safety reasons. Don't retry blindly. Surface it, or route to a human. model_context_window_exceeded The conversation hit the model's context window limit. Compact, summarise, or trim the history, then continue. Minimal correct loop (Python) import anthropic client = anthropic.Anthropic() messages = [{"role": "user", "content": task}] while True: resp = client.messages.create( model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=4096, tools=TOOLS, messages=messages, ) messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content}) # keep full history if resp.stop_reason == "tool_use": results = [] for block in resp.content: if block.type == "tool_use": try: out = run_tool(block.name, block.input) results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id, "content": out}) except ToolError as e: # structured error, not a crash results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id, "content": str(e), "is_error": True}) messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results}) # ALL results in ONE message continue if resp.stop_reason == "max_tokens": raise TruncatedResponse() # or continue with a higher cap break # end_turn / stop_sequence / refusal ⚠️ Classic loop anti-patterns (distractor fodder) Parsing text to decide when to stop (e.g. looking for "DONE" or "I have completed"). Use stop_reason. A fixed iteration cap as the main stop condition. max_turns is a safety net, not the control logic. Stopping when the response contains text. A tool_use response can contain text and tool calls. Dropping the assistant message before appending tool_result. Every result must follow the assistant turn that contains its tool_use. Running only the first tool_use when the model asked for several in parallel. Claude Code's own loop Inside Claude Code the loop works in three phases: gather context → take action → verify results, repeated until done. The harness adds behaviour between iterations: permission checks before each tool call, PreToolUse/PostToolUse hooks around it, a Stop hook when the model tries to end, and auto-compaction as the window fills. Related: tool_choice Value Behaviour Use when {"type":"auto"} The model decides whether to call a tool (default with tools). Normal agent loops. {"type":"any"} The model must call some tool, and picks which. You need structured output, but the right schema varies by input. {"type":"tool","name":"x"} Forces that specific tool. Guaranteed structured extraction with one schema, or a mandatory first step. {"type":"none"} No tool calls allowed. A final text-only answer. 💡 RememberA JSON schema (through tool input or --json-schema) guarantees shape, not correctness. You still need semantic validation, such as "do line items add up to the total?", with a retry that tells the model the specific error.

If the match isn't unique, add surrounding context or fall back to Read + Write. Glob Find files by name pattern (**/*.test.ts) Use it to find files by path or name. NotebookEdit Edit Jupyter cells Skill Invoke a skill The model can call it on its own, based on the skill's description. mcp__<server>__<tool> Tools from MCP servers Named like mcp__github__create_issue. docs.keywords: CLAUDE.md memory rules import hierarchy init
docs.text: CLAUDE.md files are instructions loaded into context automatically at session start. Use them for things Claude should always know: build and test commands, conventions, architecture notes, and things it must never do. The hierarchy Level Location Shared via git? Use for Enterprise / managed OS-level managed policy path (set by IT) Org-wide Company standards that apply to everyone User ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md ❌ personal Your preferences in every project Project ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md ✅ committed Team conventions, commands, architecture Project-local ./CLAUDE.local.md ❌ gitignored Your personal notes for this repo Subdirectory ./packages/api/CLAUDE.md ✅ Loaded on demand when Claude works with files in that directory Files above the working directory (walking up to root) load at startup. Files in subdirectories load lazily when Claude reads files there. More specific instructions take precedence when they conflict. Imports and modular rules # CLAUDE.md See @README.md for an overview and @package.json for npm scripts. ## Conventions - Use pnpm, never npm. - Run `pnpm test --filter <pkg>` before committing. - @docs/api-conventions.md - @~/.claude/my-personal-prefs.md # imports can point to home dir @path imports pull other files in. They resolve recursively up to 4 hops deep, and aren't evaluated inside code spans or blocks. .claude/rules/*.md holds modular rule files. Add paths: frontmatter to scope a rule so it loads only when Claude touches matching files: --- paths: - "src/api/**/*.ts" - "**/*.test.ts" --- - All API handlers must validate input with zod. - Tests use vitest; never import from jest. Commands for memory /init: analyse the repo and generate a starter CLAUDE.md. /memory: open and edit the loaded memory files, and see which ones are active. ⚠️ Traps "A new teammate doesn't get the instructions" → they were in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md (personal), not the committed project CLAUDE.md. CLAUDE.md is advisory: it's text in the prompt. If something must happen every time (formatting, blocking a command), use a hook or a permission rule. Keep it concise. A bloated CLAUDE.md wastes context on every turn. Move rarely-needed procedures into skills and directory-specific rules into .claude/rules/ with paths:.

docs.text: Settings files and precedence (highest wins) Managed settings (managed-settings.json, deployed by IT or MDM). Can't be overridden. Command-line arguments (--permission-mode, --allowedTools, --model…), for this session only Local project .claude/settings.local.json: personal, gitignored Shared project .claude/settings.json: committed for the team User ~/.claude/settings.json: your defaults in every project Permission arrays (allow/deny) are merged across levels. A deny anywhere wins. A realistic .claude/settings.json { "permissions": { "allow": [ "Bash(npm run test:*)", "Bash(npm run lint)", "Read(./src/**)", "mcp__github__get_issue" ], "ask": ["Bash(git push:*)"], "deny": [ "Read(./.env)", "Read(./.env.*)", "Read(./secrets/**)", "Bash(curl:*)", "Bash(rm -rf:*)" ], "defaultMode": "default", "additionalDirectories": ["../shared-lib"] }, "env": { "NODE_ENV": "development" }, "hooks": { "...": "see Hooks section" }, "enabledPlugins": {} } Permission rule syntax Rule Matches Bash Any bash command Bash(npm run test:*) Commands starting with npm run test (prefix match) Read(./.env) / Edit(src/**) File paths (gitignore-style globs) WebFetch(domain:example.com) Fetches to that domain mcp__github / mcp__github__* All tools from the github MCP server Agent(Explore) A specific subagent type Evaluation order: deny → ask → allow. The first matching category decides. Anything unmatched falls back to the current permission mode. Permission modes (cycle with Shift+Tab) Mode Behaviour Typical use default Prompts the first time each tool or command is used Normal interactive work acceptEdits Auto-approves file edits. Still asks for risky bash. Trusted refactors you're watching plan Read-only: Claude explores and proposes a plan without editing Complex or unfamiliar changes; review the approach first auto A classifier approves routine actions and blocks risky ones Long autonomous runs with a safety net (newer; availability varies) dontAsk Denies anything not pre-approved, without prompting Locked-down, non-interactive runs bypassPermissions Skips all prompts (--dangerously-skip-permissions) Only in isolated containers or VMs 🎯 Exam lens"Never let Claude read .env in this repo, for everyone" → deny rule in the committed .claude/settings.json (or managed settings for the whole org). Not a line in CLAUDE.md, and not settings.local.json (personal).

docs.keywords: SKILL.md skills custom commands frontmatter context fork allowed-tools ARGUMENTS
docs.text: A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md: reusable instructions (and optional scripts or reference files) that load only when needed. Custom slash commands (.claude/commands/*.md) have been merged into skills. Both create a /name command, and old command files still work. Locations .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md: project, committed, shared with the team ~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md: personal, available in all projects Plugins can ship skills too (namespaced plugin:skill) Anatomy .claude/skills/review-pr/ ├── SKILL.md # required ├── checklist.md # loaded only if SKILL.md references it └── scripts/diff.sh # can be executed by the skill # SKILL.md --- name: review-pr description: Review a pull request for correctness and security. Use when the user asks to review a PR. argument-hint: [pr-number] allowed-tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash(gh pr diff:*) context: fork # run in an isolated subagent context disable-model-invocation: true # only the user can trigger it via /review-pr --- Review PR #$ARGUMENTS. 1. Run `gh pr diff $ARGUMENTS`. 2. Check against @checklist.md. 3. Report findings as: file:line — severity — issue — fix. Frontmatter Effect name, description The description is what the model uses to decide when to auto-invoke. Make it specific. allowed-tools Tools pre-approved while the skill runs (restricts or expands what it can do without prompting) argument-hint Autocomplete hint. The arguments arrive in $ARGUMENTS. context: fork Runs in a separate subagent context, so verbose output doesn't pollute the main conversation disable-model-invocation The model can't trigger it on its own; the user must type /name model Override the model for this skill 💡 Progressive disclosureAt startup only each skill's name and description sit in context. The body loads when the skill is invoked, and referenced files load only if needed. That's why skills scale better than piling everything into CLAUDE.md.

docs.keywords: subagents agents Agent Task tool isolated context parallel Explore Plan coordinator
docs.text: A subagent is a separate Claude instance with its own context window, its own system prompt, and a restricted tool set. The main agent delegates through the Agent tool and gets back only the final result. Defining one # .claude/agents/security-reviewer.md (project) or ~/.claude/agents/ (personal) --- name: security-reviewer description: Reviews diffs for injection, authz and secrets issues. Use proactively after changes to auth or payment code. tools: Read, Grep, Glob # least privilege — read-only model: sonnet # sonnet | opus | haiku | inherit --- You are a senior application-security reviewer. Return findings as JSON: [{file, line, severity, issue, fix}]. Report only issues you can point to in code. Other ways to define them: /agents (interactive), claude --agents '{...json...}' (session-only), or the agents option in the Agent SDK. Built-in subagents Explore: fast, read-only codebase search Plan: researches the codebase to build a plan in plan mode general-purpose: multi-step tasks with the full tool set Key facts ⚠️ #1 trap: subagents do NOT inherit the parent's context A subagent sees only its own system prompt and the prompt string the parent passes. It doesn't see the conversation history. If the coordinator found that "the bug is in auth/session.ts, line 88", it must write that into the delegation prompt. Parallelism: several Agent calls in a single assistant response run concurrently, e.g. one subagent per independent module. Context protection: the subagent reads 40 files, and only a summary returns. This is the main reason to use them. Hub-and-spoke: a coordinator decomposes the work, delegates, aggregates, and validates. Subagents don't talk to each other; all communication goes through the coordinator. No nesting: in Claude Code, subagents can't spawn their own subagents. Structured hand-off: ask subagents for structured output (with sources or file:line) so the coordinator can merge results without losing provenance. Independent review: a fresh subagent (or separate session) reviews better than the same session reviewing its own work, because it doesn't share the author's assumptions. 🎯 Exam lens"A coordinator's final report misses whole areas" → the root cause is usually task decomposition (the coordinator's scope was too narrow), not the subagents. Fix the coordinator's decomposition instead of adding another layer.

docs.keywords: hooks PreToolUse PostToolUse Stop UserPromptSubmit SessionStart exit code 2 deterministic
docs.text: Hooks are shell commands (or LLM prompts) that the harness runs at fixed lifecycle events. Unlike CLAUDE.md instructions, they always run. Use them for anything that must happen every single time. Events Event Fires Can block? Typical use SessionStart Session start or resume – Inject context (git branch, open tickets) UserPromptSubmit Before a prompt is processed ✅ Validate prompts, add context, block secrets PreToolUse Before a tool runs (after Claude builds its params) ✅ Block dangerous commands, enforce policy, change input PermissionRequest When a permission dialog would show ✅ Auto-allow or deny programmatically PostToolUse After a tool succeeds feedback Auto-format, lint, run tests, normalise data Notification Claude needs input or is idle – Desktop or Slack notification Stop The main agent tries to finish ✅ "Tests must pass before stopping" SubagentStop A subagent finishes ✅ Validate subagent output PreCompact Before compaction – Back up the transcript, preserve key facts SessionEnd Session ends – Cleanup, logging Configuration (in any settings.json) { "hooks": { "PreToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Bash", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "\"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/.claude/hooks/block-dangerous.sh" }] } ], "PostToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Edit|Write", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "npx prettier --write \"$(jq -r .tool_input.file_path)\"" }] } ] } } matcher is a regex on the tool name (Edit|Write, mcp__github__.*). The hook receives JSON on stdin: session_id, transcript_path, cwd, hook_event_name, tool_name, tool_input (plus tool_response for PostToolUse). Exit codes — memorise these Exit code Meaning 0 Success. Execution continues. stdout can return JSON for fine-grained control (and for SessionStart/UserPromptSubmit, it's added as context). 2 Blocking error. The action is blocked and stderr is fed back to Claude so it can adjust. other Non-blocking error. stderr is shown to the user and execution continues. #!/usr/bin/env bash — .claude/hooks/block-dangerous.sh cmd=$(jq -r '.tool_input.command') if echo "$cmd" | grep -qE 'rm -rf /|git push --force|DROP TABLE'; then echo "Blocked by policy: $cmd. Use a safer alternative." >&2 exit 2 # block + tell Claude why fi exit 0 Advanced JSON output, e.g. PreToolUse: {"hookSpecificOutput":{"hookEventName":"PreToolUse","permissionDecision":"deny","permissionDecisionReason":"…"}} with allow / deny / ask. Stop-hook loop guardWhen a Stop hook blocks (forcing Claude to keep working), check the stop_hook_active field in its input. Otherwise it can block forever. 🎯 Exam lens: prompt vs hook"Claude sometimes forgets to run the formatter" or "refunds over $500 must never be auto-approved" → a hook (deterministic), not a stronger CLAUDE.md instruction (probabilistic). For business rules with financial or compliance impact, the answer is programmatic enforcement.

docs.keywords: MCP model context protocol .mcp.json scope stdio http claude mcp add env var
docs.text: The Model Context Protocol lets Claude Code use tools, resources, and prompts from external servers (GitHub, Jira, databases, Sentry, internal APIs) without custom glue code. Scopes Scope Stored in Visible to local (default) ~/.claude.json under the project path Only you, only this project project .mcp.json at the repo root (committed) The whole team (each member approves it on first use) user ~/.claude.json Only you, in every project Adding servers # Remote HTTP server (recommended transport for remote) claude mcp add --transport http sentry https://mcp.sentry.dev/mcp # Local stdio server, shared with the team claude mcp add --transport stdio --scope project db -- npx -y @bytebase/dbhub --dsn "$DB_URL" claude mcp list | get <name> | remove <name> claude mcp add-json <name> '{...}' # inside a session: /mcp → status + OAuth login .mcp.json with environment-variable expansion { "mcpServers": { "github": { "type": "http", "url": "https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${GITHUB_TOKEN}" } }, "jira": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@acme/jira-mcp"], "env": { "JIRA_URL": "${JIRA_URL:-https://acme.atlassian.net}", "JIRA_TOKEN": "${JIRA_TOKEN}" } } } } ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} keep secrets out of git while the config itself is shared. MCP primitives Tools: callable actions, named mcp__server__tool. Resources: readable data you can @-mention (e.g. @github:issue://123). They give the agent a catalogue without many exploratory tool calls. Prompts: show up as slash commands (/mcp__server__prompt). 🎯 Exam lens Claude picks the wrong tool → improve the tool descriptions (purpose, inputs, when to use it vs. similar tools). Don't add a routing classifier. Too many tools (e.g. 18) degrade selection → give each agent only the tools its role needs. Tool errors should be structured (isError, error category, whether it's retryable, a human-readable message). Never return an empty success for a failure. An empty result for a valid query is not an error. Team-wide server → .mcp.json (project scope). Personal experiment → local or user scope.

docs.keywords: claude -p print headless output-format json stream-json json-schema allowedTools max-turns CI GitHub Actions
docs.text: claude -p "<prompt>" (print mode) runs the full agent loop non-interactively and exits. It's the basis for scripts, cron jobs, and CI pipelines. CLI flags you must know Flag Purpose -p, --print Non-interactive (headless) mode --output-format text|json|stream-json json gives one result object (result, session_id, total_cost_usd, num_turns, is_error…). stream-json gives newline-delimited events. --json-schema '<schema>' Validated structured output matching a JSON Schema (with --output-format json) --input-format stream-json Stream input messages through stdin --allowedTools / --disallowedTools Pre-approve or forbid tools: "Read,Grep,Bash(npm test:*)" --permission-mode default, acceptEdits, plan, bypassPermissions… --max-turns N Cap agent iterations (a safety net) --model Choose the model (alias or full ID) --append-system-prompt / --system-prompt Add to, or replace, the system prompt --mcp-config file.json Load MCP servers for this run --agents '{json}' Define subagents for this session -c, --continue Continue the most recent session in this directory -r, --resume [id] Resume a specific session (or pick from a list) --fork-session With --resume/--continue: branch into a new session ID instead of appending --add-dir Grant access to extra directories --verbose Full turn-by-turn logging --dangerously-skip-permissions Same as bypassPermissions. Only use it in sandboxes. Examples # Pipe input, get JSON back git diff main | claude -p "Review this diff for bugs" --output-format json | jq -r .result # Guaranteed structured output claude -p "Extract all TODOs in src/ with file and line" \ --output-format json \ --json-schema '{"type":"object","properties":{"todos":{"type":"array","items":{"type":"object","properties":{"file":{"type":"string"},"line":{"type":"integer"},"text":{"type":"string"}},"required":["file","line","text"]}}},"required":["todos"]}' # Locked-down CI run claude -p "Fix the failing lint errors" \ --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash(npm run lint:*)" --max-turns 10 GitHub Actions # .github/workflows/claude-review.yml on: { pull_request: { types: [opened, synchronize] } } jobs: review: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 with: anthropic_api_key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }} prompt: "Review this PR against CLAUDE.md standards. Comment only on real issues." claude_args: "--max-turns 8 --allowedTools Read,Grep,Glob" Run /install-github-app once to set it up. After that, team members can @claude in issues and PRs. 🎯 Exam lens: CI design Put review standards in the project CLAUDE.md so CI and humans share them. Use a separate session or instance to review code that Claude generated. Self-review in the same context is weaker. Use --output-format json (plus --json-schema) so a script can post inline comments. On re-runs, pass in previous findings to avoid duplicate comments. Message Batches API (≈50% cheaper, up to 24 h, matched by custom_id) suits non-blocking overnight jobs, not pre-merge checks that developers wait on.

headings: Recommended workflow: Explore → Plan → Implement → Commit
docs.keywords: context window compaction /compact /clear resume fork checkpoint rewind plan mode lost in the middle
docs.text: What fills the context window System prompt + tool definitions (including MCP tools) + CLAUDE.md files + skill descriptions + the conversation + every tool result. Big tool outputs are the usual culprit. Check with /context. Strategies Technique When /clear Switching to an unrelated task. Stale context hurts quality. /compact [focus] A long task you want to continue. You decide what the summary keeps. Auto-compaction Triggers automatically near the limit. Project CLAUDE.md is re-loaded afterwards, but conversation-only details may be lost. Subagents Offload verbose exploration. Only the summary comes back. Scratchpad / notes files Persist key findings (decisions, exact IDs, amounts) to a file that survives compaction and new sessions. Trim tool outputs Have tools or hooks return only the relevant fields, not 40-field records. "Case facts" block Keep critical facts (customer ID, amounts, dates) in a structured block, not buried in prose, so summaries don't drop exact values. 💡 Lost in the middleModels attend most reliably to the start and end of long inputs. Put key findings and instructions at the beginning or end, and use clear section headers. Sessions claude --continue: pick up the latest conversation. claude --resume: choose one. --fork-session: try two approaches from the same starting point without clobbering the original. When resuming after files have changed, tell Claude what changed. Stale tool results in history can mislead it. Sometimes a new session with a summary is better than resuming. Checkpoints & rewind Claude Code checkpoints file edits automatically. EscEsc or /rewind restores code, conversation, or both to an earlier point. LimitationCheckpoints track Claude's file-edit tools only. They don't undo bash side effects (rm, DB migrations, git push) or external changes. Git is still your real safety net. Recommended workflow: Explore → Plan → Implement → Commit Explore in plan mode. Read files without editing. Plan: have Claude write a plan (extended thinking helps). Review and edit it. Implement step by step, verifying with tests. TDD works well: write the tests first, then iterate until they pass. Commit and open a PR. Plan mode is worth it for multi-file, architectural, or ambiguous changes. For a clear one-line fix, go straight to editing.

docs.keywords: Agent SDK query ClaudeAgentOptions ClaudeSDKClient python typescript
docs.text: The Agent SDK exposes Claude Code's harness (loop, tools, permissions, hooks, subagents, MCP, compaction) as a library, so you can build your own agents: support bots, research agents, data pipelines. from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions options = ClaudeAgentOptions( system_prompt="You are a careful refactoring agent.", allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "Edit", "Bash"], permission_mode="acceptEdits", max_turns=15, cwd="/repo", setting_sources=["project"], # load CLAUDE.md / .claude settings from the repo mcp_servers={"jira": {...}}, agents={"tester": AgentDefinition(description="Runs and fixes tests", tools=["Bash","Read","Edit"], prompt="...")}, ) async for msg in query(prompt="Rename UserSvc to UserService everywhere", options=options): print(msg) # AssistantMessage, ToolUse…, finally ResultMessage(subtype="success" | "error_max_turns" …) query(): one-shot async iterator. ClaudeSDKClient: multi-turn conversation with interrupts. Custom tools: define in-process with @tool + create_sdk_mcp_server, then reference them as mcp__name__tool. Hooks: Python or TS callbacks for PreToolUse, PostToolUse, etc. Same semantics as the CLI. Sessions: resume=session_id, fork_session=True. can_use_tool callback: custom permission logic at runtime.

docs.keywords: plugins marketplace output styles statusline which mechanism comparison
docs.text: A plugin bundles skills, commands, subagents, hooks, and MCP servers into one installable unit (.claude-plugin/plugin.json). Install with /plugin marketplace add owner/repo and then /plugin install name@marketplace, or pin them for a team through enabledPlugins in settings. Decision table Need Use Why not the alternative Facts and conventions Claude should always know CLAUDE.md (or .claude/rules) A skill loads only when invoked Rules for one directory or file type .claude/rules/ with paths: or a subdirectory CLAUDE.md Keeps the root CLAUDE.md lean A repeatable multi-step procedure Skill / slash command CLAUDE.md would bloat every turn Verbose or parallel work, isolated context, a specialist role Subagent (or skill with context: fork) The main context stays clean Must happen 100% of the time Hook Prompts are probabilistic Allow or forbid specific actions or files Permission rules (managed for the org) Enforced by the harness, not the model Talk to Jira, GitHub, a DB, an internal API MCP server Standard, reusable, permissionable Distribute all of the above to many teams Plugin (+ marketplace) One versioned bundle Automation in pipelines claude -p / GitHub Action / Agent SDK No interactive prompts Also good to know: output styles (change Claude's response style or persona), a custom status line (/statusline), sandboxed bash (filesystem and network isolation), and extended thinking for hard planning.

docs.keywords: traps distractors cheat sheet
docs.text: Tempting distractor Better answer Detect completion by parsing "Task complete" in text Loop on stop_reason == "tool_use", stop on end_turn A hard iteration cap is the stop condition stop_reason drives the loop. max_turns is only a safety net. Subagent "already knows" what the coordinator found Pass all needed context explicitly in the delegation prompt Make the CLAUDE.md instruction stronger ("ALWAYS!!") A hook or permission rule for anything mandatory Put team config in settings.local.json / ~/.claude Commit .claude/settings.json, CLAUDE.md, .mcp.json Add a classifier or routing layer for wrong tool picks Fix the tool descriptions first, and reduce tool count per agent Same session reviews its own code A separate instance or subagent with fresh context JSON schema means the data is correct A schema guarantees structure. Add semantic validation and a retry with the specific error. Retry until the field appears If the data isn't in the source, retrying won't help. Make the field nullable or "not found". Batch API for pre-merge checks Batch is for non-blocking, latency-tolerant work Escalate on negative sentiment or low self-reported confidence Escalate on explicit request, policy gaps, or inability to make progress Return a generic "error" or empty list on failure Structured error: category, retryable?, message. Distinguish "no results" from "failed". Summarise everything into prose Keep exact values (amounts, IDs, dates) in a structured facts block Invented flags like --headless, --batch, --ci The real ones: -p, --output-format, --json-schema, --allowedTools, --max-turns Rewind undoes everything Checkpoints don't undo bash side effects or remote actions

docs.keywords: quiz practice questions
docs.text: Score: 0 / 0 answered (of 10) 1 · [D1] Your custom agent loop sometimes stops after the model says "Let me check the database" without calling a tool, and sometimes keeps looping after the answer is complete. What's the fix? C. stop_reason is the structured signal. Text parsing (A, D) is brittle: tool_use responses often contain text too. A fixed cap (B) either cuts work short or wastes calls. 2 · [D2] Your team wants Claude Code to never read .env files in a repo, for every developer. Best approach? A. Permission rules are enforced by the harness, and the shared settings file reaches every teammate. B is advisory only. C is personal and gitignored. D affects git, not Claude's file access. 3 · [D1] A coordinator delegates "fix the bug" to a subagent after spending 20 turns finding that the bug is in session.ts:88. The subagent starts searching the whole repo from scratch. Why? D. Subagents start with fresh, isolated context. The coordinator has to pass the file, line, and reasoning explicitly. 4 · [D2] Developers complain that Claude Code sometimes forgets to run Prettier after editing files. What's the most reliable fix? B. Hooks are deterministic and run every time. Prompt instructions (A) are probabilistic, and C still depends on someone remembering. 5 · [D2] A hook script must block a Bash command and tell Claude why, so it can try another approach. How should it exit? C. Exit code 2 is the blocking error, and stderr is fed back to Claude. Other non-zero codes are non-blocking and stderr goes only to the user. 6 · [D2] The team wants a shared Jira MCP server that every developer gets automatically, without committing the API token. What should they do? A. Project scope (.mcp.json) shares the config, and ${VAR} expansion keeps secrets in each developer's environment. B's default scope is local, so each developer would have to set it up manually. 7 · [D2] A CI job needs Claude to output review findings in a strict JSON shape that a script turns into inline PR comments. Which invocation fits? B. -p is headless mode. --output-format json plus --json-schema gives validated structured output. --headless and --batch are invented flags. 8 · [D5] After two hours on one task, Claude starts forgetting the exact refund amount agreed earlier. Which change helps most? D. Progressive summarisation loses exact values. Persisting them in a structured block or file, plus a focused compaction, preserves them. B throws away context; A only delays the problem. 9 · [D2] You have a 12-step release checklist that's only needed a few times a month. Where should it live? C. Skills load on demand (progressive disclosure), are shared through git, and can be invoked as /release. A would bloat every session; B is personal; hooks aren't procedures. 10 · [D1] Claude finishes generating code and you want a high-quality review before merge. What's the best setup? B. An independent reviewer doesn't share the author's assumptions. A is self-review bias; D is wrong for blocking pre-merge checks. 📚 Source of truthVerify details against the official docs at code.claude.com/docs and docs.claude.com. Claude Code ships fast, and flags and features change.

docs.section: Harness engineering: the system around the model
docs.text: AI · Topic 5 · Exam domains D1 · D2 · D5 Harness engineering: the system around the model The model proposes; the harness disposes. A harness is all the code and configuration around an LLM: the loop that calls it, the context it sees, the tools it may use, the permissions that gate them, the checks that verify its work, and the traces that tell you what happened. With the same model, the harness often decides whether an agent is a toy or a teammate. This page builds one up, from concepts to a tested ~200-line implementation. D1 · D2 · D5 loop, configuration, reliability 3 animated diagrams 17 offline tests behind the code ≈ 80 min read

docs.keywords: harness definition model engine car scaffolding agent = model + harness
docs.text: The one-line definitionAgent = Model + Harness. The model is the engine. The harness is everything else that makes it a car you can trust on a road: steering (the loop), fuel (context), controls (tools), brakes (permissions and budgets), dashboard (traces), and inspection (verification and evals). Only the orange box is the model. Every blue box is harness code you own. A denied call at the gate goes back to the model as an error result, so it can choose another way. Why harness engineering matters The same model gives very different results in different harnesses. Agent benchmark scores depend heavily on the scaffold: the tools offered, how errors are reported, and when the agent is allowed to stop. Reliability lives in the harness. Budgets, approvals, sandboxes, and verification are code. The model can't promise them. Cost and latency live in the harness. Caching, context hygiene, and model routing are harness decisions. Harnesses are what you can change today. You can't retrain the model, but you can ship a better harness this afternoon.
