If you are building on the raw Messages API, every row above is yours to write. Sections 3–8 show how.

docs.section: 3. The control loop: when to call, continue, and stop
docs.keywords: budgets turns tokens dollars stop conditions max_tokens refusal retries backoff task budget
docs.text: Concern Good practice Stop conditions Finish on end_turn after verification; stop on refusal; continue on max_tokens (or raise it); resend on pause_turn (server tools). Budgets Cap turns, output tokens, dollars, and wall-clock time. All are hard stops in code. A model-visible task budget (beta task_budget) lets the model pace itself instead of being cut off. Warn before cutting off A few turns before the limit, append a short instruction ("3 turns left, wrap up") so the run ends with a summary instead of mid-edit. Retries The SDKs already retry 408/409/429/5xx and connection errors with backoff (2 retries by default). Add your own retry only around tools, and only for idempotent ones. Loop detection Notice the same tool called with the same arguments repeatedly, and intervene (a message, or a stop). Streaming & long turns Stream large outputs to avoid HTTP timeouts. Show progress, and let users interrupt.

docs.section: 4. Context assembly, caching and append-only transcripts
docs.keywords: prompt caching cache_control prefix append-only preserved thinking compaction system message mid-session
docs.text: Every request re-sends the whole conversation, and the API processes it as one long prefix: tools → system → messages. Prompt caching makes the unchanged part of that prefix cheap and fast. That leads to the most important context rule in harness engineering: keep the past byte-for-byte stable and only append. The green bar is the cache hit. Appending keeps it long; editing anything earlier cuts it at the edit. Rules for the context builder Freeze the prefixTools in a deterministic order, a system prompt with no timestamps or request IDs, and memory files loaded once per session. Append, never rewriteDon't edit or delete earlier messages. Beyond caching, newer models bind their thinking blocks to the exact conversation that produced them. Editing history invalidates them (and new API accounts get a 400 for it). Mid-session instructions as messagesTo change instructions, append a {"role": "system", …} message instead of editing the top-level system prompt. It preserves the cache and carries operator authority. Shrink with server-side toolsUse API compaction (compact_20260112) or context editing (clear_tool_uses_20250919) rather than hand-rewriting history. Cap tool output before it is appended. MeasureLog usage.cache_read_input_tokens. If it stays at zero, something in your prefix changes every request. """Cache-friendly request layout: stable things first, growing things last, never edit the past.""" import anthropic from my_tools import TOOLS as MY_TOOLS # your tool definitions client = anthropic.Anthropic() SYSTEM_PROMPT = open("SYSTEM.md").read() # frozen for the whole session: no timestamps! TOOLS = sorted(MY_TOOLS, key=lambda t: t["name"]) # deterministic order on every request messages = [] # append-only transcript def turn(user_text: str): messages.append({"role": "user", "content": user_text}) response = client.messages.create( model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=16000, tools=TOOLS, # 1. rendered first system=[{"type": "text", "text": SYSTEM_PROMPT, "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}}], # 2. breakpoint: tools + system cache_control={"type": "ephemeral"}, # 3. auto-cache the growing tail messages=messages, ) messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content}) u = response.usage print(f"cache read={u.cache_read_input_tokens} written={u.cache_creation_input_tokens} " f"uncached={u.input_tokens}") # watch your hit rate return response def add_instruction(text: str): """Mid-session instruction WITHOUT editing the system prompt (keeps the cache valid).""" messages.append({"role": "system", "content": text})

headings: Claude Code: permissions and hooks in .claude/settings.json
docs.keywords: permissions allow ask deny hooks PreToolUse PostToolUse Stop exit code 2 sandbox defense in depth settings.json
docs.text: Safety in a harness is layered, so no single mistake is catastrophic. 1 · Prompt Tells the model the rules. Soft: it guides most behaviour, but it can be forgotten or overridden by injected text. 2 · Permissions Allow / ask / deny per tool or command pattern, checked by code before execution. 3 · Hooks Your scripts run at lifecycle events and can block, modify, or add context. Deterministic. 4 · Sandbox Even if everything above fails, the process can't reach what it isn't given: files, network, credentials. Claude Code: permissions and hooks in .claude/settings.json { "permissions": { "allow": ["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "Bash(npm test:*)", "Bash(git diff:*)", "Bash(git status)"], "ask": ["Bash(git push:*)", "WebFetch"], "deny": ["Read(./.env)", "Read(./secrets/**)", "Bash(curl:*)"] }, "hooks": { "PreToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Bash", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "python3 .claude/hooks/block_dangerous.py" }] } ], "PostToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Edit|Write", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "jq -r '.tool_input.file_path' | xargs npx prettier --write" }] } ], "Stop": [ { "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "python3 .claude/hooks/stop_until_tests_pass.py" }] } ] } } Hook event Fires Typical use PreToolUse Before a tool runs Block dangerous commands; validate arguments; enforce branch policies PostToolUse After a tool succeeds Auto-format edited files; run linters; log UserPromptSubmit When the user sends a prompt Add context; block prompts containing secrets Stop / SubagentStop When the agent wants to finish Refuse to stop until tests pass SessionStart / PreCompact Session start; before compaction Load project state; save notes before history is summarised A command hook receives the event as JSON on stdin. Exit 0 lets it proceed. Exit 2 blocks it, and stderr is fed back to Claude so it can adapt: #!/usr/bin/env python3 """Claude Code PreToolUse hook: block destructive shell commands. Claude Code sends the pending tool call as JSON on stdin. Exit 0 = allow. Exit 2 = block; stderr is shown to Claude so it can choose another way. """ import json import re import sys DANGEROUS = [ r"\brm\s+-rf\s+(/|~|\$HOME)", r"\bgit\s+push\b.*--force", r"\bDROP\s+(TABLE|DATABASE)\b", r"\bcurl\b[^|]*\|\s*(ba|z)?sh\b", ] event = json.load(sys.stdin) command = event.get("tool_input", {}).get("command", "") for pattern in DANGEROUS: if re.search(pattern, command, re.IGNORECASE): print(f"Blocked by policy: '{command}' matches {pattern}. Use a safer alternative.", file=sys.stderr) sys.exit(2) sys.exit(0) 🎯 Exam lens: prompt vs hook"Claude must always run the formatter after editing" → a PostToolUse hook, not a CLAUDE.md line. "Never touch .env" → a deny permission rule plus a sandbox, not just an instruction. Instructions are for judgment; hooks and permissions are for guarantees.

docs.keywords: verification tests feedback loop stop hook definition of done self check judge
docs.text: The highest-leverage thing a harness can do is give the agent a way to check its own work, and refuse to finish until the check passes. Models are good at fixing a failure they can see. Two failed checks feed their error output back to the agent; on the third attempt the light turns green and only then does the run finish. Verifier Strength Watch out for Rules / code (tests, linters, type-checkers, schema validation) Fast, cheap, objective Only as good as the tests; agents may "fix" tests instead of code, so protect test files Visual (screenshots of UI) Catches layout and rendering bugs Needs a browser tool and a clear spec LLM as judge (a separate reviewer with a rubric) Handles fuzzy quality (tone, completeness) Costs tokens; calibrate against human grades Human review The final authority for high-stakes changes Slow; save it for what matters In Claude Code, a Stop hook turns this into policy. Exit 2 blocks the stop and hands the failure output back to Claude: #!/usr/bin/env python3 """Claude Code Stop hook: the agent may not finish while the tests fail. Exit 2 blocks the stop and feeds stderr back to Claude, so it keeps working. """ import json import subprocess import sys event = json.load(sys.stdin) if event.get("stop_hook_active"): # we already sent it back once: don't loop forever sys.exit(0) tests = subprocess.run(["npm", "test", "--silent"], capture_output=True, text=True) if tests.returncode != 0: print("Tests are failing. Fix them before finishing:\n" + (tests.stdout + tests.stderr)[-2000:], file=sys.stderr) sys.exit(2) sys.exit(0) ⚠️ TrapA Stop hook that always blocks creates an endless loop. Check stop_hook_active (as above), or count attempts and give up after N.

docs.section: 7. Build it: a complete mini harness (tested)
docs.keywords: mini harness python implementation policy budget hooks trace compaction tested
docs.text:
Everything above in one file, on the raw Messages API. It's small enough to read in ten minutes, and it is covered by offline tests with a scripted fake client: the deny pattern, the pre-hook block, a human "no", secret redaction, a failed-then-passed verification, the budget warning, and the trace are all exercised. """A small but complete agent harness. The model only proposes actions. Everything in this file is the harness: loop control, budgets, permissions, hooks, context hygiene, verification and tracing. """ import json import re import subprocess import time from dataclasses import dataclass, field from pathlib import Path from typing import Callable, Optional import anthropic MODEL = "claude-opus-5-5" @dataclass class Tool: name: str description: str input_schema: dict fn: Callable[..., str] risk: str = "read" # read | write | exec def spec(self) -> dict: return {"name": self.name, "description": self.description, "input_schema": self.input_schema} @dataclass class Policy: """Permission rules: deny patterns first, then a default per risk level.""" read: str = "allow" write: str = "ask" exec: str = "ask" deny_patterns: tuple[str, ...] = ("rm -rf", "git push --force", "| sh", ".env") def decide(self, tool: Tool, args: dict) -> str: blob = json.dumps(args) if any(p in blob for p in self.deny_patterns): return "deny" return getattr(self, tool.risk) @dataclass class Budget: max_turns: int = 30 max_output_tokens: int = 300_000 turns: int = 0 output_tokens: int = 0 def charge(self, usage) -> None: self.turns += 1 self.output_tokens += usage.output_tokens @property def turns_left(self) -> int: return self.max_turns - self.turns def exhausted(self) -> bool: return self.turns_left <= 0 or self.output_tokens >= self.max_output_tokens PreHook = Callable[[str, dict], Optional[str]] # return a reason to block, or None PostHook = Callable[[str, dict, str], str] # may rewrite the output (e.g. redact) def ask_human(name: str, args: dict) -> bool: return input(f"Allow {name} {json.dumps(args)[:200]}? [y/N] ").strip().lower() == "y" @dataclass class Harness: tools: list[Tool] system: str client: anthropic.Anthropic = field(default_factory=anthropic.Anthropic) policy: Policy = field(default_factory=Policy) budget: Budget = field(default_factory=Budget) approve: Callable[[str, dict], bool] = ask_human pre_hooks: list[PreHook] = field(default_factory=list) post_hooks: list[PostHook] = field(default_factory=list) verify: Optional[Callable[[], Optional[str]]] = None # failure text, or None when OK max_result_chars: int = 10_000 trace_path: Path = Path("trace.jsonl") # -- observability --------------------------------------------------------------- def trace(self, event: str, **data) -> None: with self.trace_path.open("a") as f: f.write(json.dumps({"ts": time.time(), "event": event, **data}, default=str) + "
") # -- one model call: stable prefix for caching, server-side compaction ------------- def call_model(self, messages: list): return self.client.beta.messages.create( model=MODEL, max_tokens=16000, betas=["compact-2026-01-12"], context_management={"edits": [{"type": "compact_20260112"}]}, system=[{"type": "text", "text": self.system, "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}}], # caches tools + system tools=[t.spec() for t in self.tools], # same order on every call messages=messages, ) # -- one tool call: hooks -> permission -> execute -> post-process ----------------- def run_tool(self, block) -> dict: def result(text: str, error: bool = False) -> dict: self.trace("tool", name=block.name, error=error, chars=len(text)) return {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id, "content": text, "is_error": error} tool = next((t for t in self.tools if t.name == block.name), None) if tool is None: return result(f"Unknown tool '{block.name}'.", error=True) for hook in self.pre_hooks: # deterministic guardrails reason = hook(block.name, block.input) if reason: return result(f"Blocked by policy: {reason}", error=True) decision = self.policy.decide(tool, block.input) if decision == "deny" or (decision == "ask" and not self.approve(block.name, block.input)): return result(f"Permission denied for {block.name}. Try a different approach.", error=True) try: output = tool.fn(**block.input) except Exception as exc: # errors become information return result(f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}", error=True) for hook in self.post_hooks: output = hook(block.name, block.input, output) if len(output) > self.max_result_chars: # context hygiene cut = len(output) - self.max_result_chars output = output[: self.max_result_chars] + f"
[... {cut} more chars not shown]" return result(output) # -- the loop ---------------------------------------------------------------------- def run(self, task: str) -> str: messages: list = [{"role": "user", "content": task}] self.trace("start", task=task) while not self.budget.exhausted(): response = self.call_model(messages) self.budget.charge(response.usage) self.trace("model", stop_reason=response.stop_reason, output_tokens=response.usage.output_tokens) messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content}) # append-only if response.stop_reason == "tool_use": calls = [b for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use"] messages.append({"role": "user", "content": [self.run_tool(b) for b in calls]}) if self.budget.turns_left == 3: # warn instead of cutting off messages.append({"role": "system", "content": "3 turns left. Finish the current step and summarise."}) continue if response.stop_reason == "max_tokens": messages.append({"role": "user", "content": "Continue exactly where you stopped."}) continue if response.stop_reason == "refusal": self.trace("refusal") return "The model declined this task." failure = self.verify() if self.verify else None # end_turn: check before accepting if failure is None: self.trace("done", turns=self.budget.turns) return "".join(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text") self.trace("verify_failed", details=failure[:500]) messages.append({"role": "user", "content": f"Verification failed. Fix this before finishing:
{failure}"}) self.trace("budget_exhausted", turns=self.budget.turns) return "Stopped: budget exhausted." # ---- wiring it up ------------------------------------------------------------------- def read_file(path: str) -> str: return Path(path).read_text() def write_file(path: str, content: str) -> str: Path(path).write_text(content) return f"Wrote {len(content)} chars to {path}" def run_command(command: str) -> str: p = subprocess.run(command, shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=120) return f"exit={p.returncode}
{p.stdout}{p.stderr}" def tests_pass() -> Optional[str]: p = subprocess.run(["pytest", "-q"], capture_output=True, text=True) return None if p.returncode == 0 else (p.stdout + p.stderr)[-3000:] def protect_main_branch(name: str, args: dict) -> Optional[str]: if name == "run_command" and re.search(r"git (commit|push).* main ", args.get("command", "")): return "Never commit or push to main. Create a feature branch." return None def redact_secrets(name: str, args: dict, output: str) -> str: return re.sub(r"sk-[A-Za-z0-9_-]{20,}", "[REDACTED]", output) PATH = {"type": "string", "description": "Path relative to the repo root."} TOOLS = [ Tool("read_file", "Read a UTF-8 text file.", {"type": "object", "properties": {"path": PATH}, "required": ["path"]}, read_file, "read"), Tool("write_file", "Create or overwrite a file with the given content.", {"type": "object", "properties": {"path": PATH, "content": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["path", "content"]}, write_file, "write"), Tool("run_command", "Run a shell command in the repo (120 s timeout). Returns exit code and output.", {"type": "object", "properties": {"command": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["command"]}, run_command, "exec"), ] if __name__ == "__main__": harness = Harness( tools=TOOLS, system="You are a careful coding agent. Make the smallest change that makes the tests pass.", pre_hooks=[protect_main_branch], post_hooks=[redact_secrets], verify=tests_pass, ) print(harness.run("The test test_parse_date is failing. Find the cause and fix it.")) Harness feature Where in the code Bounded loop & budgets Budget, while not self.budget.exhausted() Warn before the end appended role: "system" message at 3 turns left Permissions (allow / ask / deny) Policy.decide per risk level + deny patterns Deterministic guardrails pre_hooks (e.g. protect_main_branch) Output hygiene post_hooks (redaction) + max_result_chars cap Errors as information every failure becomes is_error: true, never an exception Caching & compaction cache_control on the system block; server-side compact_20260112 Append-only transcript only messages.append(...), never edits Verification before done verify() on end_turn; failures re-enter as feedback Observability trace() → trace.jsonl

docs.section: 8. Or rent the harness: the Claude Agent SDK
docs.keywords: claude agent sdk hooks can_use_tool allowed_tools permission_mode HookMatcher
docs.text: The Agent SDK gives you Claude Code's harness (built-in tools, loop, compaction, subagents, sessions) and lets you plug in your own policy as Python callbacks: """The same guardrails, programmatically, with the Claude Agent SDK.""" import asyncio from claude_agent_sdk import (ClaudeAgentOptions, HookMatcher, PermissionResultAllow, PermissionResultDeny, ResultMessage, query) async def block_dangerous(input_data, tool_use_id, context): """PreToolUse hook: runs before every Bash call, can deny it.""" command = input_data["tool_input"].get("command", "") if "rm -rf" in command or "--force" in command: return {"hookSpecificOutput": { "hookEventName": "PreToolUse", "permissionDecision": "deny", "permissionDecisionReason": "Destructive command blocked by policy.", }} return {} async def can_use_tool(tool_name, tool_input, context): """Called for tools that are NOT pre-approved in allowed_tools.""" if tool_name in ("Write", "Edit") and not tool_input.get("file_path", "").startswith("/repo/"): return PermissionResultDeny(message="Only files inside /repo may be changed.") return PermissionResultAllow() options = ClaudeAgentOptions( cwd="/repo", allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "Bash"], # pre-approved; never reach can_use_tool can_use_tool=can_use_tool, # decides Write/Edit hooks={"PreToolUse": [HookMatcher(matcher="Bash", hooks=[block_dangerous])]}, max_turns=40, max_budget_usd=3.00, ) async def main() -> None: async for message in query(prompt="Upgrade the date library and fix what breaks.", options=options): if isinstance(message, ResultMessage): print(message.subtype, message.num_turns, message.total_cost_usd) if __name__ == "__main__": asyncio.run(main()) ⚠️ A subtle ordering ruleTools listed in allowed_tools are pre-approved: they never reach your can_use_tool callback. Put a tool there only if you never want to inspect its calls. Hooks still run for pre-approved tools, which is why the dangerous-command check above is a PreToolUse hook. Permission mode Behaviour default Ask for anything not allowed by rules acceptEdits Auto-approve file edits; still ask for other risky tools plan Read-only exploration and planning; no changes dontAsk Never prompt: anything not pre-approved is denied auto A classifier approves low-risk calls and escalates the rest bypassPermissions No checks at all. Only inside a disposable sandbox

docs.section: 9. Long-running agents: work that spans many context windows
docs.keywords: long running progress file feature list initializer git checkpoints multi session
docs.text: Some jobs (building an app, a large migration) can't finish in one context window. Each new session starts with no memory, so the harness must make the environment carry the state: Initializer sessionSets up the project, writes a structured feature list (all items "failing"), an init.sh to start the app, and a progress file, then makes the first git commit. Each working session starts by orientingRead the progress file and git log, run init.sh, and run a smoke test to confirm nothing is broken before starting. One feature at a timePick the highest-priority failing item, implement it, and verify it end to end. Leave a clean stateMark the item passing only after verification, commit with a descriptive message, and update the progress notes for the next session. # features.json (the agent may only flip "passes"; never delete or edit tests) [{"id": "auth-01", "description": "User can sign up with email", "passes": true}, {"id": "auth-02", "description": "Password reset email is sent", "passes": false}] # progress.md (written at the end of every session) ## Session 14 - Done: auth-01 (signup), verified in browser; commit 3f2a91c - Next: auth-02. Mail sender stub exists in src/mail.ts - Gotcha: run `npm run db:reset` before e2e tests 💡 Why JSON for the feature list?Structured files are harder for the model to "accidentally" rewrite than prose, and easy for the harness to check (e.g. a hook that rejects edits removing items).

docs.section: 10. Observability: you can't fix what you can't see
docs.keywords: tracing logging metrics opentelemetry tokens cost cache hit rate
docs.text: Signal Why it matters Source Full transcript / trace per run Debugging starts by reading what the agent saw and did JSONL events, SDK message stream, Claude Code transcripts Tokens in/out, cache read/write Cost and cache health response.usage Cost per completed task The real unit economics (a cheap call that needs 5 retries isn't cheap) Sum per run ÷ successes Turns per task, tool error rate Spot confusing tools and loops Trace events Permission denials, hook blocks Policy too tight, or agent misbehaving Harness logs; ResultMessage.permission_denials in the SDK Claude Code can export usage metrics via OpenTelemetry, so teams can track usage and cost in their existing dashboards.

docs.keywords: evals pass@k pass^k graders regression ablation transcripts
docs.text: Every harness change (new tool description, different compaction threshold, new hook) can help one task and hurt another. Treat the harness like any other software: a fixed task set, automatic graders, and a number you track. Collect tasksReal requests with a checkable outcome (tests that must pass, expected fields, a rubric). Start with 20–50; grow from production failures. Grade automaticallyCode checks first; LLM judges with a rubric for fuzzy quality; humans to calibrate the judges. Run each task several timesAgents are stochastic. One run tells you little. Change one thing at a timeAn ablation shows which harness component actually moved the score. Read transcripts of failuresThe fix is usually visible: a misleading tool description, a missing error message, a context flood. """Measuring an agent harness: run every task k times, report pass@k AND pass^k.""" from math import comb from statistics import mean def pass_at_k(n: int, c: int, k: int) -> float: """P(at least one of k attempts succeeds), from n trials with c successes.""" if n - c < k: return 1.0 return 1 - comb(n - c, k) / comb(n, k) def pass_hat_k(n: int, c: int, k: int) -> float: """P(ALL k attempts succeed): the reliability number users actually feel.""" return comb(c, k) / comb(n, k) def evaluate(tasks: list[dict], run_agent, grade, trials: int = 5, k: int = 3) -> dict: per_task = [] for task in tasks: successes = sum(bool(grade(task, run_agent(task["prompt"]))) for _ in range(trials)) per_task.append({"id": task["id"], "successes": successes}) return { f"pass@{k}": mean(pass_at_k(trials, t["successes"], k) for t in per_task), f"pass^{k}": mean(pass_hat_k(trials, t["successes"], k) for t in per_task), "per_task": per_task, } 🎯 pass@k vs pass^kpass@k: at least one of k tries succeeds. That's fine when a human picks the best attempt. pass^k: all k tries succeed. That's what matters for an unattended agent that runs every day. A harness with 60% per-try success has pass@3 ≈ 94% but pass^3 ≈ 22%.

docs.keywords: anti patterns mistakes checklist
docs.text: Anti-pattern Do instead Safety rules only in the prompt Permissions + hooks + sandbox; the prompt explains why Timestamps or per-request data in the system prompt Frozen prefix; volatile data in the latest message Editing or deleting earlier messages Append-only; server-side compaction and context editing; role: "system" messages for new instructions Raising exceptions on tool failure is_error results with actionable text Unbounded loops Turn, token, dollar, and time budgets, plus a warning before the cut-off Accepting "done" at face value Verification on end_turn; Stop hooks Dumping whole files or results into context Caps, pagination, just-in-time reads, subagents Judging changes from one lucky run Repeated trials; pass^k; ablations bypassPermissions on a laptop with real credentials Only in disposable, network-restricted sandboxes

Score: 0 / 0 answered 1 · Your team requires that every edited file is auto-formatted. What's the most reliable implementation in Claude Code? B. Hooks are deterministic and run every time. Instructions are followed most of the time, which isn't a guarantee. 2 · Cache reads stay at zero across requests in a long session. Most likely cause? C. Caching is a prefix match. Any byte change invalidates everything after it, so a changing system prompt or tool order silently kills the cache. 3 · Mid-session, you need to tell the agent "the deploy freeze is now active." What's the best harness technique? A. Appending keeps the cached prefix (and thinking blocks) valid and carries operator authority. Editing or deleting history breaks both. 4 · A Stop hook runs tests and exits 2 on failure. Users report the agent sometimes never stops. Fix? D. The hook should block once and then let the agent stop (reporting the failure) rather than loop indefinitely. 5 · In the Agent SDK you added "Write" to allowed_tools and wrote a can_use_tool callback to block writes outside the repo. Writes outside the repo still happen. Why? B. Remove Write from allowed_tools (or enforce the rule in a PreToolUse hook, which runs regardless). 6 · An agent passes a task 60% of the time per run. For an unattended nightly job, which metric best reflects the risk? C. Consistency matters when no human picks the best attempt. pass^k measures reliability; pass@k measures "can it ever do it". 7 · A multi-day build agent keeps redoing finished work in each new session. Best harness fix? A. New sessions start with no memory, so the harness must make the environment carry the state. 8 · Which change belongs in the harness rather than the model prompt? D. Output caps and redaction must happen every time, before the model sees the data, so they're code. The others are guidance.

docs.section: How LLMs work: from your text to the model's reply
docs.text: AI · Topic 2 · Foundations How LLMs work: from your text to the model's reply Follow a single prompt through the whole pipeline: text becomes tokens, tokens become vectors, vectors pass through dozens of transformer layers, and a probability distribution produces the next token. That step repeats until the model stops. Once you see the pipeline, things like token limits, temperature, prompt caching, stop_reason and "lost in the middle" make sense. Why it matters explains cost, latency, limits & failure modes ≈ 45–60 min read

docs.keywords: overview pipeline steps
docs.text: Every request to Claude (or any decoder-only LLM) goes through these stages. The rest of the page explains each one. Assemble the promptSystem prompt, tool definitions, and the conversation history are formatted into one long text sequence with role markers. TokenizeThe text is split into sub-word pieces (tokens), and each piece is mapped to an integer ID from a fixed vocabulary. EmbedEach token ID looks up a row in the embedding matrix and becomes a vector of thousands of numbers. Add positionPosition information is mixed in (e.g. RoPE), so the model knows token order. Transformer layers (×N)Each layer runs self-attention (tokens exchange information) and then an MLP (per-token processing), with residual connections. The vectors become richer at each layer. Unembed → logitsThe final vector at the last position is projected to one score per vocabulary token. Softmax + samplingTemperature, top-k and top-p shape the probabilities, and one token is picked. Repeat (autoregression)The new token is appended and the model runs again for the next one. A KV cache avoids recomputing earlier tokens. StopGeneration ends on an end-of-turn token, a stop sequence, max_tokens, or a tool call. That reason is the API's stop_reason. Detokenize & streamToken IDs are turned back into text and streamed to you, or parsed into structured blocks such as tool_use. One sentence to rememberAn LLM is a function that takes a sequence of tokens and returns a probability distribution over the next token. Everything else (chat, tool use, reasoning) comes from calling that function repeatedly.

docs.keywords: chat template system prompt roles stateless messages
docs.text: The model doesn't receive "a message". It receives one flat sequence. The API turns your structured request (system prompt, tools, messages[]) into that sequence using a chat template: special marker tokens that separate roles and turns. # What you send (Messages API) system: "You are a concise geography tutor." messages: [ {role: "user", content: "What is the capital of France?"} ] # Conceptually, what the model sees (marker names are illustrative) <system>You are a concise geography tutor.</system> <user>What is the capital of France?</user> <assistant> ← the model continues writing from here Tool definitions (name, description, JSON schema) are serialised into the prompt too. That's why tool descriptions use up tokens and strongly influence which tool is picked. The model is stateless. It has no memory between API calls. Every request resends the entire conversation, including earlier tool results. "Memory" features (CLAUDE.md, conversation history) work by putting text back into the prompt. Prefill: if you end with a partial assistant message, the model simply continues it. That's because generation is just "continue this sequence". 🎯 Why this mattersLong conversations get more expensive and slower every turn, because the whole history is reprocessed. Hence context management, compaction, and prompt caching.

headings: How the vocabulary is built: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE)
docs.keywords: tokens tokenizer BPE byte pair encoding vocabulary token id
docs.text: Neural networks process numbers, not characters. A tokenizer splits text into tokens (frequent sub-word chunks) and maps each one to an integer token ID in a fixed vocabulary. Worked example The text The capital of France is through the public GPT-2 tokenizer (Claude uses its own tokenizer with different IDs, but the idea is identical): The464 capital3139 of286 France4881 is318 Notice the leading space is part of the token (" capital"), and common words are a single token. Rare words get split: something like "tokenization" might become "token" + "ization", and an unusual name might become several fragments. How the vocabulary is built: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) Start with the 256 possible bytes (UTF-8), so any text, emoji, or language can be represented. Nothing is ever "unknown". Count the most frequent adjacent pair in a huge training corpus (e.g. t + h) and merge it into a new token th. Repeat tens of thousands of times: th+e → the, ␣+the → ␣the … Stop at the target vocabulary size (typically ~32k–200k tokens). At inference time, the same merges are applied to your text. Consequences you can observe Effect Why English ≈ 3–4 characters per token. Code, JSON, and many non-English languages use more tokens per word. The vocabulary was built mostly from frequent English patterns Limits and pricing are in tokens (context window, max_tokens, $ per million tokens) The token is the model's unit of work Models can struggle to count letters ("how many r's in strawberry?") or reverse strings The model sees straw|berry as chunks, not individual characters Arithmetic on long numbers can be shaky Numbers are split into irregular chunks Different models give different token counts for the same text Each model family has its own tokenizer. Use the API's token-counting endpoint, or usage in responses, for exact counts.

docs.keywords: embedding matrix vector d_model lookup semantic
docs.text: A token ID like 4881 is just an index. The model's first layer is an embedding matrix of shape [vocab_size × d_model]. Each token ID selects one row, and that row is the token's embedding vector. vocab_size = 50,257 d_model = 768 # GPT-2 small (public numbers) E = embedding matrix, shape [50257 × 768] # learned during training " France" → id 4881 → E[4881] = [ 0.021, -0.113, 0.487, …, 0.064 ] # 768 numbers Prompt of 5 tokens → matrix X of shape [5 × 768] "Embedding" and "vector" are the same thing here. An embedding is a vector (a list of numbers). "Tokens → embeddings → vectors" is really one step: tokens → embedding vectors. The values aren't hand-designed. They're learned in training, so tokens used in similar contexts end up with similar vectors (" Paris" near " Lyon", " king" near " queen"). Individual dimensions usually don't mean anything readable. Meaning is spread across many dimensions. At this point each vector knows only which token it is, not its position or context. " bank" has the same starting vector in "river bank" and "bank account". The transformer layers fix that. Real model sizes (public open models) Model Vocab size d_model (vector size) Layers Attention heads Context GPT-2 small 50,257 768 12 12 1,024 Llama 2 7B 32,000 4,096 32 32 4,096 Llama 3 8B 128,256 4,096 32 32 (8 KV heads) 8,192 Anthropic doesn't publish Claude's architecture details. Frontier models are far larger, with context windows of hundreds of thousands of tokens or more, but the pipeline is the same. ⚠️ Don't confuse the two kinds of "embeddings" Token embeddings (this step): internal to the LLM, one vector per token, the input to the transformer. Text embeddings for search/RAG: a separate embedding model (e.g. Voyage AI) turns a whole sentence or document into one vector. Similar meaning gives a high cosine similarity. These vectors go in a vector database for retrieval. The LLM never sees them; it only sees the retrieved text placed into the prompt.

docs.keywords: positional encoding RoPE rotary order
docs.text: Attention (next step) is order-blind on its own. "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would look identical. Models inject position information: Method How Used by Sinusoidal (absolute) Add a fixed sine/cosine pattern per position to each embedding Original Transformer (2017) Learned absolute Add a learned vector per position (position 0, 1, 2 …) GPT-2 RoPE (rotary) Rotate the query and key vectors by an angle proportional to position. Attention then depends on relative distance. Llama and most modern LLMs How position is encoded also limits how long a context the model handles well. Extending context windows mostly comes down to positional-encoding tricks plus training on long documents.

docs.keywords: attention query key value QKV softmax causal mask multi-head
docs.text: Self-attention lets every token look at earlier tokens and pull in relevant information. It's how " it" in "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired" picks up meaning from " animal". Query, Key, Value From each token's vector x, the layer computes three new vectors using learned weight matrices: Query q = x·WQ: "what am I looking for?" Key k = x·WK: "what do I contain?" Value v = x·WV: "what will I hand over if you attend to me?" Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( Q·Kᵀ / √d_k + causal_mask ) · V 1. Score: each query · every key → how relevant is token j to token i? 2. Scale: ÷ √d_k → keeps softmax from saturating 3. Mask: −∞ for future positions → token i may only see tokens ≤ i (causal) 4. Softmax: scores → weights summing to 1 5. Mix: weighted sum of value vectors → the new information for token i Attention weights for " it" (illustrative) Weight The 0.02 animal 0.61 didn't cross 0.08 the street 0.14 because 0.05 it (itself) 0.10 Causal mask: a token can't attend to future tokens. That's what makes the model a next-token predictor, and it's why generation goes left to right. Multi-head: the layer runs many attention "heads" in parallel (e.g. 32), each with its own WQ, WK, WV. Different heads learn different relationships: syntax, coreference, copying, and so on. Their outputs are concatenated and projected back to d_model. Cost: every token is compared with every earlier token, so attention compute grows quadratically with sequence length (O(n²)). Long contexts are expensive. 💡 Connects to "lost in the middle"Attention is a learned, soft weighting, not perfect lookup. In very long prompts, models tend to use information at the start and end more reliably than in the middle. That's why you put key instructions and facts at the beginning or end, under clear headers.

docs.section: 7. Step 5b — The transformer block, stacked N times
docs.keywords: transformer block MLP feed-forward residual stream layer norm MoE
docs.text: A pre-norm transformer block. Real models stack dozens of these, each with its own weights. MLP (feed-forward network): applied to each token's vector independently. It expands to roughly 4× width, applies a non-linearity, and projects back. Most of a model's parameters, and much of its "factual knowledge", live here. Residual stream: each sub-layer adds its output to the running vector rather than replacing it. Think of the vector as a shared workspace that every layer reads from and writes to. Layer norm keeps the numbers in a stable range so deep stacks train well. Depth builds meaning: early layers handle syntax and local patterns; middle and late layers handle meaning, facts, and the plan for the next token. By the last layer, the vector at the final position encodes "what should come next". Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) variants replace the single MLP with many expert MLPs and a router that sends each token to a few of them. That gives more total parameters at similar compute per token.

docs.keywords: logits unembedding softmax probability distribution
docs.text: After the last layer, take the vector at the last position (the token right before the one being predicted). Multiply it by the unembedding matrix [d_model × vocab_size] to get one raw score, or logit, per vocabulary token. h_last shape [4096] logits = h_last · W_U shape [vocab_size] e.g. 128,256 scores probs = softmax(logits / T) all positive, sum to 1 For "The capital of France is", the top of the distribution might look like this: Next token Logit Probability (T = 1) Paris 9.0 ≈ 0.87 a 6.2 ≈ 0.05 the 5.8 ≈ 0.04 located 5.1 ≈ 0.02 … 128k others low tiny The model doesn't output an answer. It outputs a distribution. Picking from it is a separate step.

docs.keywords: temperature top_p top_k greedy sampling deterministic
docs.text: Control What it does Effect Temperature (T) Divide logits by T before softmax T < 1 sharpens toward the top token (focused, consistent). T > 1 flattens the distribution (diverse, riskier). T → 0 ≈ greedy (always the top token). top-k Keep only the k most likely tokens Cuts off the long tail of unlikely tokens top-p (nucleus) Keep the smallest set whose cumulative probability ≥ p Adapts to how confident the model is Constrained decoding Mask out tokens that would break a grammar or JSON schema The basis of guaranteed-structure outputs Temperature 1.00 top-p 1.00 Prompt: The capital of France is. Example logits; greyed-out tokens are excluded by top-p. Click "Sample" a few times, then lower or raise the temperature. Determinism caveatLow temperature makes outputs much more consistent, but even temperature 0 isn't strictly guaranteed to be bit-for-bit identical across calls on large-scale serving infrastructure. For reliability, design for validation and retries rather than assuming identical outputs.

docs.section: 10. Step 8 — The generation loop, KV cache, prefill vs decode
headings: Two phases with very different performance
docs.keywords: autoregressive KV cache prefill decode TTFT latency streaming
docs.text: One forward pass produces one token. To write a reply, the model loops: tokens = tokenize(prompt) while True: probs = model(tokens)[-1] # distribution for the next position nxt = sample(probs, T, top_p) if nxt == END_OF_TURN or hit_stop_sequence or len(out) == max_tokens: break tokens.append(nxt); out.append(nxt) stream(detokenize(nxt)) # this is why responses stream word by word KV cache The keys and values for earlier tokens don't change when a new token is added, because of the causal mask. The server caches them, so each new step only computes Q, K, and V for the single new token and attends over the cache. Without it, every step would reprocess the whole sequence. Two phases with very different performance Phase What happens Determines Prefill All input tokens are processed in parallel in one pass, and the KV cache is filled Time to first token (TTFT). Grows with prompt length. Decode Output tokens are generated one at a time, sequentially Tokens per second. Total time grows with output length. This is why output tokens cost more than input tokens: each needs its own sequential pass. Prompt caching stores the processed state (KV cache) of a stable prefix (tools, system prompt, long documents). Later requests that start with the exact same prefix skip that prefill work, so they're faster and the cached tokens are billed at a much lower rate. Put static content first and changing content last. Extended thinking is the same loop: the model generates reasoning tokens before the answer. They're real output tokens, so they cost time and money and use up the token budget.

docs.section: 11. Step 9 — Stopping, and where stop_reason comes from
docs.keywords: stop_reason end_turn max_tokens stop_sequence tool_use EOS
docs.text: What happened during generation API stop_reason The model sampled its special end-of-turn token end_turn The generated text matched one of your stop_sequences stop_sequence Output reached the max_tokens limit you set (text cut mid-thought) max_tokens The model emitted a complete tool-call block and ended its turn tool_use The prompt plus output hit the model's context window model_context_window_exceeded So stop_reason isn't something the model "decides to say". It's the server reporting which stop condition fired. Your agent loop branches on it (see the agentic loop).

docs.section: 12. Step 10 — Detokenizing, streaming and tool calls
docs.keywords: detokenize streaming tool_use parse JSON structured output
docs.text: Detokenization: token IDs are mapped back to their byte sequences and joined into text. Because a multi-byte character can be split across tokens, streaming clients buffer partial bytes. Streaming (server-sent events) sends each chunk as it's decoded. That's purely a delivery choice; the model computes the same way either way. Tool use: the model was trained to emit a special structured format when it wants a tool. The API parses that into a tool_use content block (name, input JSON, id). The model never runs anything. Your code (or Claude Code's harness) executes the tool, and the result goes back into the next prompt as a tool_result, which is tokenized like any other text. Structured output: a schema plus constrained decoding guarantees valid shape. Whether the values are correct still depends on the model, so validate the semantics.

docs.keywords: example end to end walkthrough
docs.text: User asks: "What is the capital of France?" # Stage Data at this point 1 Chat template One string: system text + <user>What is the capital of France?</user><assistant> 2 Tokenize ~20 integer IDs, e.g. […, 2061, 318, 262, 3139, 286, 4881, 30, …] 3 Embed Matrix [20 × d_model] of floats 4 + Position Same shape, now order-aware (RoPE is applied inside attention) 5 N transformer layers Same shape [20 × d_model], but each vector is now contextual. The last one "knows" an answer about France's capital is due. 6 Unembed Logits [vocab_size] for the next token 7 Softmax + sample "The" (p≈0.6) is chosen 8 Loop with KV cache " capital" → " of" → " France" → " is" → " Paris" → "." 9 Stop The end-of-turn token is sampled → stop_reason: "end_turn" 10 Detokenize / stream "The capital of France is Paris." with usage: {input_tokens: ~20, output_tokens: 7}

docs.section: 14. Where the weights come from (training, briefly)
docs.keywords: training pretraining fine-tuning RLHF constitutional AI next token prediction in-context learning
docs.text: Pre-training: the model reads trillions of tokens and learns to predict the next token. The error (cross-entropy loss) is pushed back through the network (backpropagation), nudging every weight: embeddings, attention matrices, MLPs, unembedding. This is where language, facts, and reasoning patterns come from. Post-training: supervised fine-tuning on high-quality conversations, then reinforcement learning from human and AI feedback (Anthropic uses techniques such as Constitutional AI). This turns a text predictor into a helpful, honest, harmless assistant that follows the chat format, uses tools, and knows when to stop. Inference (your API call): weights are frozen. Nothing in your prompt changes the model. "Learning" from examples in the prompt (in-context learning, few-shot) happens only within that context window and is gone on the next call. Knowledge cutoffThe model only "knows" what was in its training data up to a cutoff date. Anything newer, or private, must come in through the prompt: retrieval (RAG), tool calls, MCP, or documents you attach.

docs.section: 15. Common misconceptions, and how they connect to the exam
docs.keywords: misconceptions myths exam
docs.text: Misconception Reality Practical consequence "The model reads words or characters" It reads sub-word tokens Budget in tokens. Expect weak letter counting. "It remembers our last chat" Stateless: every call resends the full history Persist key facts (CLAUDE.md, notes files, case-facts blocks) "A bigger context means it uses everything equally" Attention is soft; the middle gets less reliable use Put critical info at the start or end, summarise, trim tool output "Embeddings and vectors are separate steps" An embedding is a vector Tokens → embedding vectors → transformer "The LLM searches my vector DB" Your code retrieves text; the LLM reads it as prompt tokens Retrieval quality is a pipeline concern, not a model one "The model runs my tools" It emits a tool_use request; your harness runs it Validate and authorise in code (hooks, permissions) "Temperature 0 means perfectly deterministic" Highly consistent, not guaranteed identical Validate outputs, add retries "A JSON schema guarantees correct data" It guarantees structure only Add semantic validation "The model learns from my corrections" Weights are frozen at inference Put corrections in the prompt or persistent memory

docs.keywords: quiz practice questions
docs.text: Score: 0 / 0 answered (of 8) 1 · What is a token embedding? B. The ID is just an index (A). C describes text embeddings used for RAG, which are a separate model. D describes the output distribution. 2 · Why does a long conversation get slower and more expensive with every turn, even when your new message is short? D. Every request resends the full conversation as input tokens. Prompt caching and compaction exist to reduce this cost. 3 · In self-attention, what does the causal mask do? A. Future positions are set to −∞ before the softmax, which makes the model a left-to-right next-token predictor. C describes top-k/top-p. 4 · You set temperature very low. What happens? C. Temperature only reshapes the softmax. The computation and the model's knowledge are unchanged, so correctness isn't guaranteed. 5 · A response ends with stop_reason: "max_tokens". What does that tell you? B. The decode loop hit the max_tokens stop condition before the end-of-turn token was sampled. 6 · Why does prompt caching require the cached content to be at the start of the prompt? D. Because of causal attention, changing an early token changes the state of every later token. An identical prefix gives identical KV state that can be reused. 7 · Why are output tokens slower and pricier than input tokens? A. Decode is sequential, with one forward pass per token, while prefill handles the whole prompt at once. 8 · In a RAG system, how does the LLM use the vector database? C. Retrieval happens outside the model. The LLM only sees the retrieved text, tokenized like the rest of the prompt. 📚 Further reading"Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., 2017); Anthropic's docs on tokens, prompt caching, streaming and extended thinking; Anthropic's interpretability research on how features are represented inside models.

Crypto & Blockchain · Topic 8 Programmable money: tokenized deposits & stablecoins Programmable money is money that carries its own rules. Instead of a person or a back-office batch job deciding when a payment happens, code on a shared ledger releases, holds, splits, or returns funds automatically when agreed conditions are met. This page explains the idea from first principles, compares the two variants banks actually use (tokenized deposits and stablecoins), shows how to build them, and walks through tested smart contracts for real use cases. 2 variants compared 7 tested smart contracts 10 use cases ≈ 60–75 min read

headings: What it lets you do that today's rails can't
docs.keywords: definition smart contract token ledger conditional
docs.text: Today, money in a bank account is a number in a database that only the bank can change. To make a payment "smart" (pay when goods arrive, sweep excess cash at 5 p.m., release salary every second), you need extra systems around the money: escrow agents, letters of credit, batch jobs, reconciliations, and people checking documents. Programmable money moves that logic next to the money. Money becomes a digital token on a shared ledger, and smart contracts (small programs on that same ledger) can hold and move tokens according to rules that every party can read and nobody can quietly change. One-sentence definitionProgrammable money = trusted digital money (a token that is a claim on a bank or a regulated issuer) + a shared ledger (one source of truth) + code that controls when and where it moves. The four building blocks 💵 Money token A digital representation of a currency claim: a tokenized deposit (a bank liability) or a stablecoin (a liability of a regulated issuer backed by reserves). 📒 Shared ledger A blockchain or other distributed ledger where balances and contract state live. Every participant sees the same state, so there is nothing to reconcile. ⚙️ Smart contract Code deployed on the ledger. It can own tokens and moves them only when its rules say so: escrow, delivery-versus-payment, sweeps, streams. 🔌 Oracles & identity Oracles bring real-world facts on-chain (shipment delivered, price, weather). Identity and KYC layers decide who may hold or receive the money. Programmable money vs programmable payments These terms get mixed up. The distinction matters to central banks and regulators: Programmable payments Programmable money Where the logic lives Outside the money, in a contract or service that decides when to move otherwise ordinary tokens Inside the token itself (e.g. a coin that can only be spent at pharmacies, or that expires) Is the money still "money"? Yes. Once paid out, the token is fully fungible Restricted. One dollar is no longer equal to another dollar Regulator view Generally favoured; preserves the singleness of money Used carefully, only for specific purposes Example on this page TradeEscrow, DvPSettlement, TreasurySweep PurposeBoundGrant (purpose-bound money: the restriction sits in a wrapper, not in the base token) 💡 Design rule of thumbKeep the base money token simple and fungible. Put business rules in separate contracts that hold the token. That way one dollar is always one dollar, and rules can change without re-issuing money. Every contract on this page follows this pattern. What it lets you do that today's rails can't Conditional settlement: pay only if X happened (delivery, approval, milestone). Atomic settlement: two legs (bond ↔ cash, USD ↔ EUR) move together or not at all. That removes counterparty settlement risk (Herstatt risk). 24/7/365, near-instant finality: no cut-off times, weekends, or batch windows. Automation without middleware: sweeps, splits, streams, and payouts run on the ledger itself. Composability: the same cash token plugs into escrow, DvP, lending, and payroll contracts. Once built, these are reusable Lego bricks. Built-in audit trail: every state change is time-stamped, signed, and shared.

docs.section: 2. Two variants: tokenized deposits vs stablecoins
docs.keywords: tokenized deposits stablecoin comparison difference CBDC
docs.text: Both put dollars (or euros, pounds, rupees…) on a programmable ledger. They differ in who owes you the money, where it can travel, and how it's regulated. 🏦 Variant 1 · Tokenized deposits A normal bank deposit, recorded as a token. It's still the bank's liability, still on its balance sheet, and still (usually) covered by deposit insurance. Typically lives on a permissioned ledger where only KYC'd customers can hold it. e.g. J.P. Morgan Kinexys · Citi Token Services · HSBC Tokenised Deposit Service 🪙 Variant 2 · Stablecoins A token issued by a regulated issuer and backed 1:1 by reserves (cash, short-term government bills). It's a claim on the issuer, not on a bank. It usually lives on public blockchains, so anyone with a wallet can hold it. e.g. USDC · USDT · PYUSD · EURC · SG-Forge EURCV Dimension Tokenized deposit Stablecoin (fiat-backed) Legal claim On the bank (a deposit) On the issuer, backed by segregated reserves Balance sheet Stays on the bank's balance sheet; the bank can keep lending against it (fractional reserve) Reserves are held 100% outside the lending book (cash / T-bills) Deposit insurance Usually yes, as for any deposit (check your jurisdiction) No; protection comes from reserve rules and redemption rights Interest Can pay interest like any deposit Regulated payment stablecoins generally can't pay interest to holders (e.g. US GENIUS Act) Typical ledger Permissioned DLT run by a bank or consortium (increasingly also public L2s) Public chains (Ethereum and its L2s, Solana, etc.) Who can hold it Only onboarded (KYC'd) clients of participating banks Anyone with a wallet, unless the address is blocklisted Cross-bank payments Need an interbank settlement step (central bank money or a shared ledger) The same token moves anywhere; no interbank step Main regulation Banking law, capital and liquidity rules Stablecoin regimes: EU MiCA, US GENIUS Act, HK, Singapore MAS, etc. Best at Wholesale and corporate banking, treasury, securities settlement, intraday liquidity Global reach, crypto/DeFi markets, cross-border retail and SME payments, machine payments Main risk Fragmentation (each bank's token is a separate island) and bank credit risk Run/de-peg risk if reserves are doubted; AML on open networks 🎯 The key insightBoth variants can run exactly the same smart contracts (escrow, DvP, sweeps), because both look like a standard ERC-20 token to the contract. What changes is who is allowed to participate and how money moves between institutions. Section 9 shows each use case built both ways.

docs.section: 3. How it works: the core loop
docs.keywords: flow animation condition oracle release
docs.text: Every programmable-money use case is a variation of one loop: lock → check condition → release (or refund). Watch a $50,000 trade payment: Funds are locked in the contract, so the seller knows the money exists and the buyer knows it can't be released early. A data feed (oracle) proves delivery, and the contract pays without anyone pressing a button. TokenizeFiat becomes a token: a bank mints deposit tokens against an account debit, or an issuer mints stablecoins against reserves. Lock (commit)The payer moves tokens into a smart contract. Now the funds are provably there but can't be spent by anyone outside the rules. ObserveThe contract gets facts: signatures from parties, an oracle's data, time passing, or another token arriving (DvP). ExecuteWhen the rule is satisfied, the contract moves tokens. Settlement and payment are the same event. Fall backEvery rule needs an exit: deadline → refund, dispute → arbiter, incident → pause. Contracts without an exit trap money. De-tokenizeThe recipient keeps the tokens for the next payment, or redeems them into a normal bank balance.

docs.keywords: deposit token bank omnibus mint burn interbank central bank Kinexys Citi HSBC Agora
docs.text: A tokenized deposit is the same deposit you already have, in a new format. When a client tokenizes $100, the bank debits the client's normal account and credits a special omnibus account. It then mints 100.00 tokens to the client's wallet on the ledger. Legally nothing changes: the bank still owes the client $100. Orange coin = Bank A's token (aUSD). It turns green (Bank B's bUSD) as it crosses banks, while the blue "R" coin settles the same amount between the two banks in central bank money. On unified-ledger designs (e.g. BIS Project Agorá) legs ② and ③ happen atomically. Lifecycle, step by step OnboardThe client is already KYC'd. The bank registers the client's wallet address on the ledger's allowlist. The wallet is often bank-custodied, with keys in an HSM or MPC. MintCore banking debits the client's DDA and credits the omnibus account. The token service calls mint(wallet, amount, coreRef). Invariant: token supply = omnibus balance. Transfer & programTokens move peer-to-peer or into contracts (escrow, DvP, sweeps) in seconds, 24/7. Cross-bankIf the payee banks elsewhere, the payer's bank token is burned (or held) and the payee's bank mints its own. The banks settle in central bank money, or both banks' tokens live on one shared ledger (Partior, Agorá, RLN-style designs). RedeemThe holder calls redeem(), the token is burned, and core banking credits the client's normal account. Real-world examples (public announcements, as of 2025) Initiative What it does J.P. Morgan Kinexys (formerly Onyx / JPM Coin) Deposit-token payments between J.P. Morgan institutional clients, 24/7, with programmable features. Reported daily volumes are in the billions. In 2025 it piloted JPMD, a USD deposit token on Base, a public Ethereum layer-2. Citi Token Services Tokenized deposits for Citi's institutional clients: 24/7 cross-border liquidity and automated trade-finance flows. HSBC Tokenised Deposit Service Tokenized deposits for corporate clients (UK, then Hong Kong) for instant 24/7 transfers between client accounts. Project Agorá (BIS + 7 central banks + 40+ private firms) Explores tokenized commercial bank deposits and wholesale central bank money on one programmable "unified ledger" for cross-border payments. Partior A shared ledger built by banks (J.P. Morgan, DBS, Standard Chartered and others) for real-time, multi-currency interbank settlement. Sample contract: TokenizedDeposit.sol A permissioned ERC-20 with the controls a bank needs: issuer-only minting tied to a core-banking reference, a KYC allowlist, account freezes, and an emergency pause. Every mint, burn, and transfer passes through one hook (_update), so the rules can't be bypassed. // SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT pragma solidity ^0.8.24; import {ERC20} from "@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC20/ERC20.sol"; import {ERC20Pausable} from "@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC20/extensions/ERC20Pausable.sol"; import {AccessControl} from "@openzeppelin/contracts/access/AccessControl.sol"; /// @title Bank A USD deposit token /// @notice Each token is a deposit liability of Bank A, mirrored 1:1 by an /// omnibus account in the core banking system. Only KYC'd customers /// (and approved contracts such as escrows) can hold or move it. contract TokenizedDeposit is ERC20, ERC20Pausable, AccessControl { bytes32 public constant ISSUER_ROLE = keccak256("ISSUER_ROLE"); // treasury ops: mint bytes32 public constant COMPLIANCE_ROLE = keccak256("COMPLIANCE_ROLE"); // allowlist, freeze mapping(address => bool) public allowlisted; mapping(address => bool) public frozen; event Minted(address indexed to, uint256 amount, bytes32 indexed coreRef); event RedemptionRequested(address indexed from, uint256 amount, bytes32 indexed accountRef); constructor(address admin) ERC20("Bank A USD Deposit", "aUSD") { _grantRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, admin); } /// Same precision as the core ledger (cents). function decimals() public pure override returns (uint8) { return 2; } /// Called only after core banking has debited the customer's account /// and credited the token omnibus account. coreRef = core transaction id. function mint(address to, uint256 amount, bytes32 coreRef) external onlyRole(ISSUER_ROLE) { _mint(to, amount); emit Minted(to, amount, coreRef); } /// Holder converts tokens back to a normal deposit. The bank's listener /// sees the event and credits the account identified by accountRef. function redeem(uint256 amount, bytes32 accountRef) external { _burn(msg.sender, amount); emit RedemptionRequested(msg.sender, amount, accountRef); } function setAllowlisted(address account, bool ok) external onlyRole(COMPLIANCE_ROLE) { allowlisted[account] = ok; } function setFrozen(address account, bool isFrozen) external onlyRole(COMPLIANCE_ROLE) { frozen[account] = isFrozen; } function pause() external onlyRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE) { _pause(); } function unpause() external onlyRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE) { _unpause(); } /// Every mint, burn and transfer passes through this hook (OpenZeppelin v5). function _update(address from, address to, uint256 value) internal override(ERC20, ERC20Pausable) { if (from != address(0)) require(allowlisted[from] && !frozen[from], "sender not permitted"); if (to != address(0)) require(allowlisted[to] && !frozen[to], "receiver not permitted"); super._update(from, to, value); } } ⚠️ GotchaSmart contracts are addresses too. To use a deposit token in an escrow or DvP contract, the bank must allowlist that contract. In practice banks maintain an approved-contract registry and only allowlist audited templates.

docs.keywords: stablecoin issuer reserve redeem mint public blockchain USDC USDT GENIUS MiCA
docs.text: A fiat-backed stablecoin is a token whose issuer promises to redeem it 1:1 for fiat and holds reserves (cash at banks and short-dated government bills) to back that promise. Because it lives on public blockchains, the same token can reach any wallet, exchange, or app worldwide without the issuer being involved in each transfer. Green "$" = fiat in the banking system; orange "x$" = the stablecoin on-chain. The issuer is only involved at mint and redeem. In between, the token moves freely across wallets, venues, and apps. Lifecycle, step by step Onboard with the issuerOnly minting and redeeming clients (corporates, exchanges, banks) are KYC'd by the issuer. Other holders are usually KYC'd by the exchange or wallet provider they use. FundThe client wires USD to the issuer's account at a reserve bank. MintThe issuer mints tokens to the client's wallet. Good designs cap minting at attested reserves (proof of reserve). CirculateThe token moves across the public chain: payments, exchanges, DeFi, bridges to other chains. Compliance relies on blocklists, on-chain analytics (Chainalysis, TRM, etc.), and the KYC done at on/off-ramps. RedeemAny eligible holder sends tokens back. The issuer burns them and pays USD out of reserves. Market & regulation snapshot (as of 2025, verify current status) Largest USD stablecoins: USDT (Tether) and USDC (Circle). Others include PYUSD (PayPal, issued by Paxos) and the euro coin EURC. Some banks issue their own, e.g. Société Générale-FORGE's EURCV and USDCV. EU, MiCA: stablecoin rules (e-money tokens and asset-referenced tokens) have applied since mid-2024. Issuers need authorisation, reserves, and redemption at par. US, GENIUS Act (2025): a federal framework for payment stablecoins. It requires 1:1 high-quality liquid reserves, regular public reserve disclosures, and a path for bank subsidiaries to issue, and it bars paying interest to holders. Asia: Singapore (MAS single-currency stablecoin framework) and Hong Kong (stablecoin issuer licensing) have dedicated regimes. Sample contract: ReserveBackedStablecoin.sol Permissionless transfers with a compliance blocklist, a hard cap that stops minting beyond attested reserves (with a staleness check on the reserve feed), and EIP-2612 permit so wallets can approve without paying gas. // SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT pragma solidity ^0.8.24; import {ERC20} from "@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC20/ERC20.sol"; import {ERC20Permit} from "@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC20/extensions/ERC20Permit.sol"; import {AccessControl} from "@openzeppelin/contracts/access/AccessControl.sol"; /// Attested reserve balance (e.g. a proof-of-reserve feed updated from the /// custodian banks' statements), in the same 6-decimal units as the token. interface IReserveFeed { function reserves() external view returns (uint256 amount, uint256 updatedAt); } /// @title Fiat-backed stablecoin /// @notice Anyone can hold and transfer it (permissionless), except addresses /// on the blocklist. New supply can never exceed attested reserves. contract ReserveBackedStablecoin is ERC20, ERC20Permit, AccessControl { bytes32 public constant MINTER_ROLE = keccak256("MINTER_ROLE"); bytes32 public constant COMPLIANCE_ROLE = keccak256("COMPLIANCE_ROLE"); IReserveFeed public immutable reserveFeed; uint256 public constant MAX_FEED_AGE = 1 days; mapping(address => bool) public blocked; event Redeemed(address indexed holder, uint256 amount); constructor(address admin, IReserveFeed feed) ERC20("Example USD", "xUSD") ERC20Permit("Example USD") { _grantRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, admin); reserveFeed = feed; } function decimals() public pure override returns (uint8) { return 6; } /// Issuer mints after fiat has arrived in the reserve account. function mint(address to, uint256 amount) external onlyRole(MINTER_ROLE) { (uint256 reserveAmount, uint256 updatedAt) = reserveFeed.reserves(); require(block.timestamp - updatedAt <= MAX_FEED_AGE, "reserve feed stale"); require(totalSupply() + amount <= reserveAmount, "exceeds reserves"); _mint(to, amount); } /// Holder sends tokens back to the issuer to be paid out in fiat off-chain. function redeem(uint256 amount) external { _burn(msg.sender, amount); emit Redeemed(msg.sender, amount); } function setBlocked(address account, bool isBlocked) external onlyRole(COMPLIANCE_ROLE) { blocked[account] = isBlocked; } function _update(address from, address to, uint256 value) internal override { require(!blocked[from] && !blocked[to], "address blocked"); super._update(from, to, value); } } Compare the two token contractsThe deposit token checks an allowlist (deny by default: you must be a known customer). The stablecoin checks a blocklist (allow by default: everyone except sanctioned addresses). That one line of difference produces most of the business differences in section 2.

docs.text: A production platform has five layers plus cross-cutting services. The same stack serves both variants; the differences are in the token layer and the ledger choice. Left: the stack from client channels down to the bank's books. Right (blue): services every layer depends on. Build roadmap Pick the money model and legal wrapperTokenized deposit (bank liability, banking licence) or stablecoin (separate issuer entity, stablecoin licence, segregated reserves)? Get the legal opinion on settlement finality: when is an on-chain transfer legally final? Choose the ledgerPermissioned (privacy, control, known validators) vs public (reach, composability, liquidity). Many banks start permissioned and add public-chain access later, as with JPMD on Base. Write the token contractStart from audited libraries (OpenZeppelin). Keep the token minimal: mint/burn roles, allow- or blocklist, freeze, pause, and possibly upgradeability behind a timelock and multi-sig. Integrate core bankingCreate the omnibus account. Mint only after a core debit and redeem only into a core credit, both idempotent. Run continuous reconciliation of supply vs omnibus. Wallets & keysCustodial wallets for most clients, with keys in HSM or MPC, policy engines (limits, approvals), and recovery procedures. Larger clients may self-custody. Programmability layerBuild a library of audited templates (escrow, DvP, sweep…) that clients parameterise. Don't let clients deploy arbitrary code against your token on day one. Oracles & eventsUse signed, multi-source data feeds for real-world conditions, and keeper bots to trigger time-based actions. ComplianceRun sanctions screening before allowlisting, transaction monitoring on-chain, Travel Rule data for transfers, and freeze/claw-back procedures. Test, audit, pilotUnit and fuzz tests, an external audit, a bug bounty, then a limited pilot (internal entities, then friendly clients) with volume caps. Key design decisions Decision Tokenized deposit (typical) Stablecoin (typical) Access model Allowlist (deny by default) Blocklist (allow by default) Decimals 2, matching the core ledger 6 (USDC convention) or 18 Privacy Private ledger, private transactions, or zero-knowledge proofs Public by default; addresses are pseudonymous Interbank / interop Shared ledger, central bank money, or token bridges between bank networks Cross-chain bridges or native multi-chain issuance (e.g. burn-and-mint transfer protocols) Gas / fees Bank-operated validators; no gas cost to clients Gas paid in the native coin; use paymasters and permit to hide it Upgradeability Proxy + timelock + bank multi-sig Proxy + timelock + multi-sig; changes are publicly visible

docs.text: Smart contracts are maybe 20% of the work. The rest is connecting them safely to the bank. These TypeScript snippets (ethers v6) show the critical paths. Mint service: core debit → tokens // mint-service.ts — turns a core-banking debit into on-chain deposit tokens import express from "express"; import { ethers } from "ethers"; import tokenAbi from "./abi/TokenizedDeposit.json"; const provider = new ethers.JsonRpcProvider(process.env.LEDGER_RPC_URL); // Production: the issuer key lives in an HSM / MPC signer, never in an env var. const issuer = new ethers.Wallet(process.env.ISSUER_KEY!, provider); const aUSD = new ethers.Contract(process.env.AUSD_ADDRESS!, tokenAbi, issuer); const app = express(); app.use(express.json()); // Core banking calls this AFTER it has debited the customer's account // and credited the token omnibus account (same amount, same reference). app.post("/core-events/tokenize", async (req, res) => { const { coreTxId, wallet, amountCents } = req.body; const coreRef = ethers.id(coreTxId); // bytes32 reference // Idempotency: the Minted event is indexed by coreRef, so retries are safe. const seen = await aUSD.queryFilter(aUSD.filters.Minted(null, null, coreRef)); if (seen.length > 0) return res.json({ status: "duplicate", txHash: seen[0].transactionHash }); const tx = await aUSD.mint(wallet, BigInt(amountCents), coreRef); const receipt = await tx.wait(); res.json({ status: "minted", txHash: receipt!.hash }); }); app.listen(8080); Redemption listener: burned tokens → core credit // redemption-listener.ts — turns burned tokens back into a normal deposit import { ethers } from "ethers"; import { coreBanking } from "./core-banking-client"; aUSD.on(aUSD.filters.RedemptionRequested(), async (from, amount, accountRef, event) => { await coreBanking.postTransfer({ debit: "TOKEN-OMNIBUS-USD", // omnibus shrinks as supply shrinks credit: ethers.decodeBytes32String(accountRef), amountCents: amount, reference: event.log.transactionHash, // idempotency key on the core side }); }); Continuous reconciliation // reconcile.ts — the one invariant a deposit-token bank must never break // on-chain totalSupply == balance of the token omnibus account in core banking async function reconcile() { const onChain: bigint = await aUSD.totalSupply(); const omnibus: bigint = BigInt(await coreBanking.balance("TOKEN-OMNIBUS-USD")); if (onChain !== omnibus) { await alerts.page("token-ops", { onChain, omnibus, diff: onChain - omnibus }); await aUSD.connect(adminSigner).pause(); // stop the bleeding, then investigate } } setInterval(reconcile, 60_000); // every minute, 24/7 Client side: pay on delivery, either variant // pay-with-escrow.ts — a corporate client's ERP pays a supplier "on delivery". // The ONLY difference between the two variants is which token address you use. import { ethers } from "ethers"; const TOKENS = { deposit: "0xA0…aUSD", // Bank A tokenized deposit (permissioned ledger) stablecoin: "0xB0…xUSD", // regulated stablecoin (public chain) } as const; export async function payOnDelivery( signer: ethers.Signer, rail: keyof typeof TOKENS, seller: string, amount: bigint, billOfLading: string, days = 30, ) { const token = new ethers.Contract(TOKENS[rail], erc20Abi, signer); const escrow = new ethers.Contract(ESCROW_ADDRESS, escrowAbi, signer); await (await token.approve(ESCROW_ADDRESS, amount)).wait(); const deadline = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) + days * 24 * 3600; const tx = await escrow.open(seller, TOKENS[rail], amount, ethers.id(billOfLading), deadline); return (await tx.wait())!.hash; } Oracle keeper: real world → contract // oracle-keeper.ts — pushes real-world events on-chain, then triggers payout // Production oracles use several signed sources (carrier + port + eBL registry). async function checkShipment(dealId: number, billOfLading: string) { const doc = await fetch(`${EBL_REGISTRY}/bills/${billOfLading}`, { headers: auth }) .then((r) => r.json()); if (doc.status === "DELIVERED" && verifySignature(doc)) { await (await oracle.setDelivered(ethers.id(billOfLading), true)).wait(); await (await escrow.release(dealId)).wait(); // seller is paid in the same minute } } ⚠️ Common failure modes Double mint on retry. Always mint with an idempotency key (here coreRef). Mint before debit. Tokens must never exist without the matching core-banking entry. Single-source oracle. One compromised API key pays out every escrow. Use multiple signed sources and limits. Hot keys in env vars. Issuer and admin keys belong in an HSM or MPC behind approval policies.
